Tour: What Is Where, and How to Run It

The parts you will use, each a link, with a live picture of what is inside one cell and a measured picture of how long a sum takes. Start here: it shows what everything is, where it lives in the repository, and the three commands that get you to a working screen.

Everything on this page is a picture of something that is already in the repository. The boxes and file names are links, so you can jump straight to the part you want. Nothing on this page needs a circuit board.

The route a learner takes: draw a small circuit, run it a step at a time, look inside one cell, and (only if you want to) see the same idea on a real board. The highlight moves along the route to show the order.

2. Inside one cell

This is the nano cell, drawn from its Verilog. Its ten gates are always there. The setting does not rewire anything: it only chooses which gate's answer comes out. Change A, B or the setting and watch the values move through the wires.

Shown at one bit so you can read it. The real cell does the same thing on every bit of a wider word at once. The pictures here are drawn by this page's own small script from the same ten equations as the Verilog; they are not the VM running.

3. What 7 + 5 looked like

The library adder was given 7 and 5 and stepped one tick at a time. The bars show how many cells were holding a value at each tick. Two values travel, then one, and the answer lands at tick 18 even though the sum itself is trivial: moving data costs time.

Measured on 10 October 2026 with the step simulator on nano/library_std/add.icm.json (27 cells); it settled after 21 ticks. My reading of the graph: the drop from two values to one is where the two inputs became one result. That reading is an interpretation of the counts, not something the simulator reports.

4. How to run it

  1. Get the files. 
    git clone https://github.com/alh-Imago/Imago-Unicell.git
cd Imago-Unicell
  2. Check what you have. It needs Python 3.12 or newer, it tells you what is missing, and it changes nothing. 
    python3 quickstart.py
  3. Open the composer in your browser. 
    python3 quickstart.py --composer

Status, 10 October 2026: steps 1 and 2 were run and work. Step 3 has not been tried in a browser yet, and the tool does not appear to need anything beyond Python and numpy, but that is not tested on a clean machine.

The Composer: A Tour With Labels

The composer is the real drawing board behind every picture in this manual. A screenshot with numbered labels shows what each part does, and the second half explains the file it saves, the ICM.

The composer is the drawing board for cell designs. You place cells on a grid, join them with wires, set what each one does, run the result a step at a time and save it. The pages so far showed single cells and tiny chains drawn by this manual. This page shows the real tool those pictures stand for, with every part labelled, and the file it saves.

Open the composer (once it is running) Composer source Design note ICM file format

The first link works only after you start the composer on your own computer: run python3 quickstart.py --composer in the repository folder (it checks what is installed and opens the page at localhost:7421/composer). On the Tour page, "How to run it" explains the installing.

1. The composer, part by part

This is a real screenshot of the composer with one of the ready-made designs loaded, the library adder (27 cells), and its adder cell selected. Click a number on the picture, or a line in the list, to see where it is. Open the screenshot full size if the small version is hard to read.

    2. The save file: ICM

    Everything you build is saved as an ICM file. It is an ordinary text file (JSON) with one record per cell: where the cell sits, what kind it is, and which of its four faces it listens on and sends out of. Nothing else is stored: no wires as such and no program. A wire is just two cells whose faces point at each other, with relay cells between them. The same file is what the VM and simulator run and what the assembler turns into Verilog for the board. Here are the real first lines of the library adder you see above, with two of its 27 records:

    { "format_version": "icm-v3",
  "name": "add",
  "description": "r = a + b (integer adder)",
  "records": [
    { "cell_id": "A",  "row": 2, "col": 1,  "core": "ram",
      "core_config": { "downstream_mask": ["s"] },
      "io_name": "a",  "super_latch_hex": "0x00000000000000000041" },
    { "cell_id": "OP", "row": 4, "col": 8,  "core": "adder",
      "core_config": { "downstream_mask": ["e"], "upstream_mask": ["w", "s"] },
      "io_name": null, "super_latch_hex": "0x00000000000000001482" },
    ... 25 more (the relay cells that make up the wires) ...
  ],
  "record_hash": "0712d99e1b35..." }
    fieldwhat it says
    cell_idThe cell's name. A and B are the inputs, OP the adder, R the output.
    row, colWhich square of the grid the cell sits on.
    coreThe kind of cell: nano, ram, adder, accumulator, comparator, latch, sequencer, branch, mul, priority, cross, corner or merge.
    core_configThe cell's settings. For OP: it sends its result east (downstream_mask) and takes its two operands from the south and west (upstream_mask). This is the whole of "what is wired to what".
    io_nameA name for a cell that is a port of the design (a, b, r). A design with named ports can be saved to the library and reused as one block.
    super_latch_hexThe same settings packed into one 80-bit word, the actual value that would be loaded into the hardware cell. For OP, 0x1482 ends in 2, which is the number for adder, and the bits above it hold the faces. The composer shows this word live as you change a cell's fields.
    record_hashA fingerprint of all the records, so a changed file can be told from an unchanged one.

    The composer's three save buttons write slightly different things:

    • Save ICM downloads the design. A plain design becomes an ICM v3 file (.icm.json; the adder above downloads as add.composed.icm.json, 27 records). A design that contains inserted blocks is saved in the ICM-VIX form (.icm-hier.json), which keeps the blocks.
    • Save flat v3 always writes plain ICM v3, with any blocks unpacked into ordinary cells.
    • Save to library keeps the design in the composer's library so you can Insert block it into another design later; its io-named cells become the block's ports.
    Because the file holds only cells and their faces, anything the composer can draw can also be written by a program. The tools folder has Python that builds designs directly (the "built by Python" list in the composer, such as the floating-point adder) and the composer simply opens them.

    3. Try it

    1. Start the composer: python3 quickstart.py --composer.
    2. In the box labelled "or a path on this machine" type nano/library_std/add.icm.json and press Open path (or pick one of the examples from the list).
    3. Click the OP cell. The Selected panel shows its fields. Change nothing yet and press Apply only if you want to see it hold.
    4. In Run / Step press Start, type 7 into a and 5 into b, then press Inject next and Run to settle. In our own run the result, 12, appeared at tick 18 and the design settled by tick 21: the same measurement shown on the Tour page.
    5. Press Save ICM, open the downloaded file (add.composed.icm.json) in any text editor and find the OP record.

    The screenshot was taken on 11 October 2026 from the composer running in a cloud session, in a desktop-width browser; your layout may differ slightly. The ICM text shown is the first part of nano/library_std/add.icm.json with the other 25 records left out. What each panel does is taken from the composer's own page text and from trying it; the field table follows docs/stripped-cell/ICM_V3_FORMAT.md and the file itself. The composer's cells here are the flex cells' picture in the VM, the same cells the earlier pages described.

    The Rest of the Flex Family

    The nano cell is one of fourteen kinds of flex cell. Here is a sentence and a link for each, grouped by what they do, plus the one thing they all share: how they hand data on. Each cell will get its own page later. This is the brief overview.

    The nano cell from the Tour is one member of a family. There are fourteen kinds of flex cell with a Verilog file of their own, plus the division core (added 12 October 2026) and two wiring tiles, cross and corner, which the generator builds from ram cells; this page gives each one a sentence and a link. Most cells now have an explainer page with live builders; where one exists, the cell's card links to it.

    1. What every flex cell shares

    Whatever a cell computes, they all hand data on the same way. A cell that has a result holds it, raising a valid signal, until the next cell takes it and answers with an ack. A global freeze stops everything where it stands. Each cell also has a width setting (18 bits on the Tang Nano 20K board). Try the freeze below, or block the sink to see an item wait.

    A simplified picture: it shows the idea (hold until taken, pass on only when the next cell is free, one item per two steps through each cell), not the exact signals of any one cell.

    2. The cells

    Logic and flow

    nano

    Ten NOR gates and a setting that picks which gate's answer comes out. The cell from the Tour.

    held A + flowing B → one result

    nano_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: The Tour →

    Logic and flow

    branch

    Compares two values and decides lower, equal or higher. What it emits for that outcome is chosen when it is set up. Either input can be a fixed value or a live stream.

    two inputs → a three-way decision

    branch_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Branching →

    Logic and flow

    merge

    Where two paths join. Pass only A, pass only B, take whichever arrives (taking turns), or wait for both and combine them with OR.

    two paths → one

    merge_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Join & Split →

    Logic and flow

    priority

    Up to four inputs compete for one output. Strict ranking, weighted turns, or a fixed repeating order. A loser keeps its item and waits.

    up to four inputs → one

    priority_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Branching →

    Logic and flow

    router

    One input out to up to two places. Which outputs are switched on is set in advance, never decided while it runs.

    one input → up to two outputs

    router_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Join & Split →

    Arithmetic

    adder

    Adds two values, or subtracts. The carry can come out on a second port.

    A, B → sum

    adder_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Maths →

    Arithmetic

    mul

    Multiplies two values. One version is built from ordinary logic, another uses the chip's multiplier blocks. The top half of the product can come out on a second port.

    A, B → product

    mul_cell_v4sa.v
    mul_cell_v4sa_dsp.v
    Explainer: Maths →

    Arithmetic

    div

    Divides one value by another and gives the quotient, and optionally the remainder on a second port. It works like long division, a set number of quotient bits per clock (chosen when the design is built), so a division is one small cell. Dividing by zero gives all ones.

    dividend, divisor → quotient (and remainder)

    div_cell_v4sa.v
    The div cell, all four families →

    Arithmetic

    compare

    Says whether a value is at least a threshold (signed), answering 1 or 0.

    value → 1 or 0

    compare_cell_v4sa.v

    Arithmetic

    accumulator

    A running count that goes up or down when it receives an up pulse or a down pulse.

    up / down pulses → count

    accumulator_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Maths →

    Arithmetic

    shift stage

    Slides all the bits left or right by an amount fixed when the design is built. Chain several for a bigger shift.

    value → shifted value

    shift_stage_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Bits →

    Arithmetic

    mask

    Cuts out chosen groups of bits by setting them to zero. An 8-bit mask says which groups.

    value → value with groups cleared

    mask_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Bits →

    Memory and sequence

    ram

    Holds a word. In fixed mode it is a constant that is always there. In flowing mode it holds a value until the next cell takes it.

    word in → word out

    ram_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Memory →

    Memory and sequence

    latch

    Remembers one bit. Set it, clear it, or toggle it.

    set / clear / toggle → one bit

    latch_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Memory →

    Memory and sequence

    sequencer

    Holds up to four small stored values (8 bits each) and moves on to the next one each time it gets an advance pulse.

    advance pulse → next stored value

    sequencer_cell_v4sa.v
    Explainer: Memory →

    Wiring

    cross

    A tile where two lanes cross without meeting: west to east and north to south straight through, with no control and no arithmetic. Each direction of travel has its own one-word slice, so the lanes never share state. One tick per tile.

    west ↔ east, north ↔ south

    No Verilog file of its own in flex: the generator builds each used direction as a ram cell.
    The cross cell, all four families → · Explainer: Routing →

    Wiring

    corner

    A tile that turns a lane: east with north and west with south (turn 0), or east with south and west with north (turn 1). Two independent turns share the square. One tick per tile.

    east ↔ north and west ↔ south, or the other pair

    No Verilog file of its own in flex: the generator builds each used direction as a ram cell.
    The corner cell, all four families → · Explainer: Routing →

    The full story of how each cell was designed, with the measured costs, is in sub/README.md. There is also an adder_chain_v4sa.v in the same folder, which strings adders together; it is a helper, not a separate kind of cell.

    Chaining Cells

    One cell on its own does one small thing. Chained, the output of one becomes the input of the next, through dedicated ports with no shared bus. Drag cells into a simple grid, type a number in, and see what comes out of the end of the chain.

    One cell on its own is not much. The power is in chaining: the output of one cell goes to the input of the next. In the flex family every connection is a dedicated point-to-point link between one output port and one input port, with no shared bus. Build a chain below and watch a number go through it.

    1. Build a chain

    Drag a cell from the palette into the grid, or click a cell and then click a slot (this works on a touch screen too). Operating cells go in the lower row, the chain. Constants (fixed ram cells) go in the upper row and feed down into the cell below them. Drag a placed block to move it.

    input port (data goes in)output port (data comes out)
    whole numbers, −131072 to 131071 (18 bits, like the Tang board)
    Scroll the grid sideways to see all of it. The result is also written under the grid.
    Examples:

    2. What to notice

    • An empty slot in the chain just carries the value along. The real composer fills the gaps between cells with relay cells in the same way, and they take time too.
    • A two-input cell waits for both. Remove the constant above an adder and the adder never fires, so nothing reaches the output. This is the two-arrival rule from the Tour.
    • The ports are fixed. An adder has two input ports (A from the left, B from above) and one output. Nothing decides at run time where a value goes; it was fixed when the chain was built.

    A simplified picture. Here each cell's output goes to its right-hand neighbour and a constant feeds down from above; the real composer can place cells anywhere and lays a route of relay cells between any two of them. Numbers are 18 bits wide and shown as signed, so they wrap around: the page computes each cell from the rules in its Verilog (adder A − B in two's complement, multiplier keeps the low half of the product, compare is a signed ≥, shift stage is a logical shift by a fixed amount, nano as in the Tour), not by running the VM.

    Arithmetic: Adder, Multiplier, Accumulator

    The arithmetic cells, opened up: the carry that travels along an add, the half of a product that does not fit, and a running total that keeps counting.

    Three cells do arithmetic: the adder, the multiplier and the accumulator. On the Chaining page they were blocks that just gave an answer. Here you can see what is inside the answer: the carry that travels along an add, the half of a product that does not fit, and a total that keeps counting.

    1. The adder: bit by bit, with a carry

    The adder adds two 18-bit words. Each column adds its two bits and the carry from the column to its right, writes the answer bit, and passes a carry on to the left. In subtract mode the cell adds A to the flipped bits of B and starts with a carry of 1, which is how two's complement subtraction works (A − B = A + NOT B + 1). Whatever carries out of the top column can come out on a second port, if the design was built with that port.

    Examples:
    Scroll the grey box sideways to see all 18 columns.
    carry into each column
    A
    B
    result (the cell's main output)
    carry out of the top column (the second port)
    0

    2. The multiplier: the half that does not fit

    Multiplying two 18-bit numbers gives a product up to 36 bits long. The cell's main output is the low half, the bottom 18 bits. The high half, the top 18 bits, is available on an optional second port. The cell treats its two inputs as plain unsigned numbers (0 to 262143). If you only use the low half, you are assuming the answer fits.

    Examples:
    high half (second port, if built)
    low half (main output)

    3. The accumulator: a total that keeps counting

    An accumulator is a running total. It has two pulse inputs, count up and count down, and each pulse changes the total by a fixed step set when it was built. In continuous mode every pulse is reported. In pulse mode nothing is reported until the total's size (ignoring sign) reaches a threshold: then the cell reports the value that crossed it and starts again from zero. As with the latch, the total always updates, but a new report can only be made once the last one has been taken.

    Try:
    0
    the running total
    nothing offered
    what the cell is reporting
    nothing yet
    what the receiver has taken

    4. What to notice

    • A carry is how a big number is built from small steps. Each column only knows two bits and a carry. A carry that ripples across all columns is why long adds take longer than short ones, and why wide adders chain carry outputs into carry inputs.
    • Subtract is add in disguise. Flip B's bits, start the carry at 1, and the same adder subtracts. When subtracting, a carry out of 1 means there was no borrow: A was at least B (read as unsigned).
    • Overflow is not an error signal. The cell gives the 18 low bits whatever happens. Two large positive numbers can give a negative result; the page flags this, but the cell itself does not.
    • Low half and high half are the same product. Throw the high half away and the answer is only right when the high half is zero. The low half is the same whether you read the numbers as signed or unsigned, which is why a signed multiply works on the Chaining page. The high half is not: it belongs to the unsigned product.
    • The accumulator is memory with arithmetic. It keeps a total, like the latch keeps a bit. In pulse mode it turns many small events into one report, which is how a counter becomes a "something has happened enough times" signal.

    A simplified picture, drawn by this page's script from the cells' Verilog (adder, multiplier, accumulator). The carry output exists only where a design asks for it, and so does the multiplier's high half; both have their own handshake. The multiplier comes in two builds, one from ordinary logic and one using the chip's multiplier blocks, which give the same numbers. The signed-overflow flag on the adder is worked out by this page, not by a port of the cell. The real cells also carry valid/ack handshakes, freeze and a configuration step, which are left out. The VM is not running here.

    Branching and Decisions

    Chained cells run straight on. Two flex cells make choices: the branch cell decides where one value goes, and the priority cell decides which of several waiting values goes next. Try both with your own numbers.

    Chained cells run straight on. Two flex cells make choices: the branch cell decides where one value goes, and the priority cell decides which of several waiting values goes next. Neither one needs a program. The choice is made by the cell, with its settings fixed beforehand.

    1. The branch cell: where does this value go?

    Each of the two inputs is set up, in advance, as either flowing (a fresh value is expected every round) or fixed (loaded once and then reused every round, like a limit). The usual use is one flowing stream against one fixed limit; two flowing inputs compare two live streams against each other. A branch cell compares its two inputs as signed numbers and gets one of three answers: low (in1 is below in2), equal or high. For each answer you have chosen in advance which of its two output ports gets the result: out1, out2, both, or neither (the value is dropped). What goes out is also chosen in advance: a constant, in1, in2, or the difference in1 − in2.

    Examples:
    out1out2

    Each value in the stream is one round. Click a row to see it in the picture.

    in1in2answerout1out2

    2. The priority cell: who goes next?

    A priority cell has four input faces (N, S, E, W) and one output. Several faces can have a value waiting at once; the cell lets exactly one through per round, and the others simply wait where they are. Only the winner is acknowledged, so nobody else loses anything. You pick how the winner is chosen:

    • Strict: the face with the best rank always wins. Rank 0 is the highest priority. A busy high-priority face can starve the others.
    • Weighted: shares in proportion to weight (0 to 3). Every waiting face earns credit equal to its weight each round, the highest credit wins, and the winner pays back the total weight of that round.
    • Sequenced: a fixed turn order, such as N, E, N, W. Only the face whose turn it is can go, even if the others have been waiting longer.

    A tie is always broken in the order N, then S, then E, then W. A face that is switched off never wins, however long it waits.

    Examples:

    Output, in the order values left the cell:

      3. What to notice

      • A branch does not run code. Its three answers and where each one goes are settings, fixed when the design is built. What varies is only the data.
      • Fixed or flowing is a setting too. A fixed input is the limit you compare against; a flowing pair needs a fresh value on each side at the same moment, so two live streams advance together or not at all.
      • Dropping a value is a choice. Setting "neither" for an answer makes the cell swallow the value silently, which is how a branch filters a stream.
      • Waiting is part of the design. In the priority cell the losers keep their values and wait; nothing is lost. Under strict priority they may wait a long time, and that is the trade you made.
      • Sequenced mode blocks on purpose. If it is E's turn and E has nothing, the cell waits for E while N and W hold their values. That makes the order certain, at the price of speed.

      A simplified picture. It shows the decision each cell makes, taken from its Verilog (branch, priority), one round at a time. The real cells also handle the valid/ack handshake and two outputs that can each be blocked separately; those are left out here. The fixed and flowing choice is shown, but not the timing of loading a fixed input: in the Verilog a fixed input must be loaded before a round can fire, and a flowing value that arrives before that is not kept, so a real design loads its fixed limit first. A fixed input is loaded again by sending it a new value, which this page does not show. Numbers are 18 bits wide and signed, like the Tang Nano 20K build. The picture is drawn by this page's script, not by running the VM.

      Joining and Splitting Paths

      Two small cells show how data meets and parts. The merge cell brings two paths into one; the router cell sends one path to up to two places. Both teach what has to wait for what.

      Two small cells that look almost too simple: merge brings two paths into one, and router sends one path to up to two places. Between them they show the two ways data can meet or part, and what has to wait for what.

      1. The merge cell: two paths become one

      The merge cell has two inputs, A and B, and one output. It has four modes, chosen when the design is built:

      • A only and B only: a plain pass-through of one input. The other input is never accepted.
      • Arbitrate: either input may go, one at a time. If both are waiting, one wins, and then the loser gets priority next time, so neither can starve. Right when the two paths are alternatives that join again.
      • Join (OR): waits for both inputs, then outputs A OR B, bit by bit, and takes both together. Right when the two paths are two halves of one item.

      Why not just OR the two whenever they arrive? Two separate items that happen to be waiting together would be fused into one wrong value. Arbitrate and Join are the safe versions of that idea.

      Try:
      A
      B
      out

        2. The router cell: one path goes to two places

        The router copies every value it takes to each of its enabled outputs, A and B. Which outputs are enabled is fixed when the design is built. It does not look at the value: it never decides, it just copies. (Deciding is the branch cell's job.)

        The rule to watch: the router takes a new value only when every enabled output has been taken by whoever it feeds. A disabled output never holds anything up. A slow or stuck receiver on one output holds back the other as well. Each receiver below can be set to accepting or stuck.

        Try:
        waiting
        router
        output A
        output B

        3. What to notice

        • Merge is where order can be lost. Two separate paths have no common clock, so the merge can only choose one at a time. That is why the page says "join" for halves of one item: it waits for both and cannot get the pairing wrong.
        • Fair is a design choice. Arbitrate hands priority to whoever just lost. Compare the strict priority cell on the Branching page, where a busy face can starve the rest.
        • Waiting is how the cells stay correct. The router never drops a value and never overwrites one. If any enabled output is stuck, everything behind it waits, and that stillness is the whole mechanism.
        • The router copies; the branch chooses. A router sends the same value to everything enabled, every time. A branch sends a value to different places depending on the value.

        A simplified picture, one round or one tick at a time, drawn by this page's script from the cells' Verilog (merge, router). The real cells also keep a one-cycle output buffer, a valid/ack handshake on every port, and freeze; the merge's items are shown as whole values and the join's OR is computed on 18-bit words. The VM is not running here. Numbers are 18 bits wide and signed for display.

        Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§08 / 28

        Crossing and Turning: Cross and Corner Tiles

        Two wiring tiles let paths cross and turn on a flat grid. They change nothing about a word; they only decide which way it leaves. Send words in and watch them cross.

        Cells sit on a flat grid and words travel between neighbours. What happens when two paths need to cross? Two wires on a flat board cannot, so there are two small wiring tiles. The cross tile lets one word go straight through while another crosses it at right angles. The corner tile turns words round a bend. Neither one changes a word. They only decide which way it leaves.

        1. One tile, four faces

        A tile has four faces, N, S, E and W, and each face can be an entry and an exit. A word that comes in by a face is held in that face's own slot and offered to the paired face on the other side. The four slots are independent, so four words can be inside at once, each going its own way. Crossing a tile costs one tick.

        • Cross: N and S are paired, and E and W are paired. A word entering at W leaves at E, one entering at N leaves at S, and so on, both ways.
        • Corner, turn 0: E is paired with N, and W is paired with S.
        • Corner, turn 1: E is paired with S, and W is paired with N. This is the mirror image, so a corner can send "E to N while W goes to S" or "E to S while W goes to N".
        Examples:
        send a word in by this faceinside the tileleft the tile by this face

        2. What to notice

        • Crossing needs no decisions. The cross tile never looks at a word. Pairs of faces are wired together, and that is the whole job. Without it, one path would have to wait for the other, or take a long detour.
        • Four slots mean no collisions. A word going W to E and a word going N to S use different slots and pass each other in the same tick. Only two words entering by the same face have to queue.
        • A stuck exit holds up only its own lane. Switch one exit to stuck: the word aimed at it waits where it is, and the other three lanes carry on. This is the same waiting rule as every other cell.
        • A corner is a cross with a bend. Both have the same four slots and the same one-tick cost. The only difference is which face each slot leads to. A corner's turn setting picks one of the two bend patterns.
        • They are routing only. The composer's routes are built from plain relay cells and these tiles. A word that goes through ten tiles has taken ten ticks, and the words that came in had their order kept.

        A simplified picture, one tick at a time. A word that arrives in a tick is held; it is offered at the next tick, and leaves when the neighbour on that side accepts it (the "accepting" switches stand for that neighbour). Taken from the Python model of the tiles, nano/corner_cell_automaton_v1.py, and the ledger entries #1035 and #1036. The real tiles also exist as Verilog (corner_cell_v4.v, corner_cell_v4c.v) and, on the flex family, a cross or corner is lowered to ram relays before the generators run; this page shows the model's behaviour, not that lowering, and the VM is not running here.

        Remembering: Latch, Sequencer and Ram

        Everything so far let go of its value as soon as it passed it on. The latch keeps one bit until it is told to change; the sequencer keeps a short list and steps through it; the ram cell holds a word in one of three ways. Press the buttons and watch what is stored and what is reported.

        Everything so far forgot its value as soon as it passed it on. Three cells keep something. The latch remembers a single bit until it is told to change; the sequencer remembers a short list and steps through it one value at a time; the ram cell holds a whole word, in one of three ways.

        1. The latch: one bit that stays

        A latch has three one-bit event inputs: set (make it 1), clear (make it 0) and toggle (flip it). Nothing else changes it. If events arrive together the order is fixed: clear beats set, and set beats toggle. After each event the cell reports its new value on its output and holds that report until the receiver takes it.

        Try pressing events one at a time. Then try switching the receiver to stuck and pressing more: the stored bit keeps changing, but the cell cannot report it, because the last report has not been taken.

        Several at once in one tick:
        0
        the stored bit
        nothing offered
        what the cell is reporting
        nothing yet
        what the receiver has taken

        2. The sequencer: a short list, one step at a time

        A sequencer is configured with up to four 8-bit values (0 to 255) and a length. It starts standing on the first value. Each advance pulse moves it on to the next value and offers that one; after the last it goes back to the start. The values come out in a fixed order, from nothing but a counter: no program, no addresses. One more rule: an advance that arrives while the last value is still waiting to be taken is ignored.

        taken

        3. The ram cell: one word, three ways to hold it

        A ram cell holds one word. What it does with that word depends on how the design was built:

        • Constant (fixed): the word is always on offer and never runs out. Any number of copies can be taken, any time. It ignores anything written to it. This is the mode the Chaining page used for its constants.
        • One-shot (flowing): a word written in is offered once. When the receiver takes it, the cell is empty again and ready for the next. While a word is waiting, a new write is refused.
        • Hold: it keeps offering its word, like a constant, and copies can be taken again and again, but a new word written in replaces it. This is the cell that behaves like a memory location: write, then read as often as you like.

        One-shot and hold can start empty or start with the configured word already inside. A constant always has it.

        –
        the stored word
        nothing offered
        what the cell is offering
        taken

        4. What to notice

        • Memory is just a value that is not thrown away. The latch keeps its bit through any number of ticks in which nothing happens. Every other cell on the earlier pages passed its value on and let go.
        • Remembering and reporting are separate. The latch updates its bit on every event, but it can only tell the next cell when its last report has been taken. Under pressure the memory is right and the report is late.
        • A fixed order needs no program. The sequencer's whole behaviour is a counter that wraps and four stored values. That is how a repeating pattern, such as the steps of a motor or a lamp, can come from a cell and not from instructions.
        • Constant, one-shot and hold are three kinds of memory. A constant never changes, a one-shot is a mailbox that empties when read, and a hold is a memory location that keeps its word until overwritten. The hardware difference is tiny; what it means for the rest of the design is large.
        • The first advance does not repeat the starting value. The cell starts standing on value 0 and the first advance steps on to value 1, which is the first one offered. Value 0 comes out last in the first lap.

        A simplified picture, one tick at a time, drawn by this page's script from the cells' Verilog (latch, sequencer, ram). The real cells carry a valid/ack handshake on every port, a freeze input and a configuration step; the page shows the stored value, the offer and the receiver's acceptance only. Each press of Advance here waits one tick for the receiver, if needed, so you can see a full cycle without counting ticks. The VM is not running. The latch holds one bit and the sequencer's values are 8 bits wide.

        Reshaping Words: Shift and Mask

        A word is a row of bits. The shift stage slides the bits along; the mask cell switches whole groups of them off. See each stage's bits, what fell off the end, and how the two together can pull a field out of a word.

        Computers work on whole words of bits at a time, and two small cells show how a word can be reshaped. The shift stage slides every bit left or right by a fixed amount. The mask cell switches whole groups of bits off. Together they can pull a piece out of a word, which is most of what unpacking data means.

        1. Build a word, shift it, mask it

        The word is 18 bits wide, like the Tang Nano 20K build. Type a number, choose a shift, and click groups of the mask to switch them off. Each stage's bits are drawn so you can see exactly what happened.

        Examples:
        Scroll the grey box sideways to see all 18 bits.
        1. the word that comes in
        ↓ shift stage
        2. after the shift stage
        ↓ mask cell: click a group to switch it off (set its mask bit)
        3. after the mask
        10pushed off the endzero filled inswitched off by the mask

        2. What to notice

        • A left shift is a multiply, until bits fall off. Sliding left by 3 multiplies by 8, as long as nothing that matters is pushed past the top. This is the cheap multiply by a power of two: no multiplier cell is needed, only wiring.
        • A right shift is a divide, with the remainder thrown away. The bits that fall off the right are gone for good.
        • This shift does not know about signs. It fills with zeros, so a negative number shifted right comes out large and positive. Keeping the sign needs a different shift.
        • The shift amount is fixed when the design is built. That is why the cell is so small: there is nothing to choose at run time. To shift by more, chain several stages.
        • The mask works on groups, not single bits. The mask word has 8 bits; at 18 bits wide each mask bit covers a group of 3 data bits, which gives six groups. Setting a mask bit sets its whole group to zero.
        • Shift then mask pulls a field out. Slide the field you want down to the bottom, then switch off the groups above it. Try the last example.

        A simplified picture, drawn by this page's script from the cells' Verilog (shift stage, mask). The real cells also have a valid/ack handshake, freeze and a configuration step; they are not shown. The mask is shown as the cell works at an 18-bit width (groups of 3 bits, six groups used out of the mask word's 8 bits). The VM is not running here.

        The VM: What It Is and How It Fits

        Every picture so far was drawn by the page itself. The VM is the real program they imitate. A map of its parts, how the two modes differ, a short Python run you can repeat, and a plain account of how far each part has been trusted.

        Every picture on the earlier pages was drawn by a small script in the page itself. The VM is the real thing those pictures imitate: a program that holds a whole design as cells, advances it one tick at a time, and lets you look at every value. This page is a map of it: what the parts are, where they live, how they connect, and how far each part has been trusted.

        1. The map

        A design goes in at the left and results come out at the right. Click any box to read what it is and where it lives. Boxes with a green outline are the ones you use every time.

        THE ROUTE OF A DESIGN
        HOW IT IS CHECKED
        LOOKING INSIDE, AND OTHER WAYS IN

        The Workbench has its own page: The Workbench: see and use the VM →

        2. The two modes

        There is one idea of a cell grid and two versions of the VM, because the hardware has two relatives.

        Standard modeMirror mode for the flex family
        Name in the codeSuperGridFlexGrid, a subclass of it
        ModelsThe original cell grid, the reference for the Arria 10 lineThe flex cells (the ones in this manual), with their valid/ack handshake
        Word widthChosen when the grid is made (default 32)Chosen to match the target: 18 for the Tang Nano 20K
        How it is trustedIt is the long-standing referenceEach flex cell was added one at a time and checked against the Verilog that the generator really produces, at word widths 4, 8, 18, 32 and 36
        When the hardware has a limit–It refuses, and says why, instead of guessing

        The rule behind this: the Verilog is the ground truth. The VM comes before any fit to a real chip, because a fit can only be proved by a VM that can mirror the target. An empty FlexGrid was first proved identical to a SuperGrid, then flex behaviour was added one cell at a time.

        3. Run it yourself

        The same engine that sits behind the composer's Run / Step panel can be driven from a few lines of Python. This loads the library adder from the Composer page, puts 7 and 5 on its two input cells and runs it at 18 bits:

        import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "tools"); sys.path.insert(0, "nano")
from flex_layout_view_v1 import Layout
from flex_layout_sim_v1 import StepSim

layout = Layout.load("nano/library_std/add.icm.json")
sim = StepSim(layout, width=18)       # the flex (mirror) VM at 18 bits
sim.inject({"A": 7, "B": 5})          # values on the two input cells
ticks = sim.run()                     # step until nothing moves any more
print("settled after", ticks, "ticks")
for line in sim.log: print(line)
print("r =", sim.seen["R"])

        Output from running exactly that, in the repository folder:

        settled after 21 ticks
tick 0: item 1 in: a=7, b=5
tick 18: out r = 12
r = [12]

        Use sim.step(1) instead of sim.run() to advance one tick at a time, and sim.state() to see every cell's value and whether it is waiting to be taken. Doing that here, the number of cells holding a value was 2 for ticks 1 to 9, 1 for ticks 10 to 17, and 0 from tick 18 on. This is the measurement drawn on the Tour page, now seen as it was taken.

        Why 18 ticks for one addition? The adder itself is one cell. The other 26 cells are the input and output ports and the relays that carry the words along the routes. The VM counts every hop, and so does the hardware.

        4. How far to trust it

        • Checked against the Verilog, cell by cell. Each flex cell's behaviour in FlexGrid was compared with the generated Verilog, run in a simulator, at several widths. That work found and fixed real faults in the Verilog itself (a cell that captured while not yet configured, and some width limits).
        • Checked against the board. Ten self-checking designs (relay chains, adders with stalls, the three priority modes, the ram hold and one-shot) run on a real Tang Nano 20K and match what FlexGrid says. That shows the cell logic and the handshake on real silicon, at 27 MHz and small sizes. It does not show capacity or speed.
        • The test suite. More than two thousand tests live under tests/vm. A full run takes hours, so they are run on demand.
        • Freeze, save and restore of a running design has only been run in simulation, never on a physical card.
        • The GPU array backend is written, but its header says it was written where no GPU was available, so the GPU path is untested there. Even in its design only the choice of which cells are ready to act is done in bulk; each cell's own logic still runs as ordinary Python.
        • Not the same as timing on a chip. The VM counts ticks of the design, not nanoseconds. The board's clock speed is a property of the chip and the build.

        Facts on this page come from the README's VM section, the file headers of nano/unicell_super_automaton_v1.py, nano/flex_grid_v1.py, tools/flex_layout_sim_v1.py, nano/gpu_array_v1.py, nano/vm_mirror_v1.py, nano/vm_introspection_v1.py, nano/vm_ai_port_v1.py and nano/walker_sim_v1.py, and from running the example above. The test and board figures are quoted from the README and the repository's own notes, not re-run for this page. The map is a summary: the real code has more parts than are drawn here.

        The Two Grids: SuperGrid and FlexGrid

        The VM comes in two versions of its cell grid: the standard one and the flex mirror. How to start each, what each accepts at other word widths, and the same small designs run on both so you can see where they agree and where they differ.

        The VM page showed the map. This page is about the two grids inside it. SuperGrid is the standard one, the long-standing reference. FlexGrid is a subclass of it that behaves like the flex cells on the Tang Nano 20K. Everything below was run on the real Python, on small designs built for the page, and the answers are what came back. The Verilog was not run for this page.

        1. Which tool uses which grid

        ToolGrid it buildsWhere you can see it
        The Composer's Start / Step / Run panelFlexGrid, through StepSimtools/flex_layout_sim_v1.py line 29: FlexGrid(recs, width=self.width)
        The WorkbenchSuperGrid, alwaysnano/workbench_v1.py: every reset and load builds VMSession(SuperGrid(...))
        VMSession.from_dsl / from_python / from_llvm / from_icm_fileSuperGridnano/vm_ai_port_v1.py
        VMSession.from_man (the mirror check against a card)SuperGridsame file; it checks the shape of the layout against the MAN file and then builds a SuperGrid
        VMSession(grid) by handwhichever grid you hand itrun for this page: VMSession(FlexGrid(records, width=18)) worked (section 5)
        So today the Composer is flex-only, and the Workbench and the mirror check are standard-only. Making the Workbench and the mirror VM able to build either grid is not done; the next pages cover both of those tools and say what that means for each.

        2. Starting a grid: the options

        Both grids are made from a list of cell records (an ICM file loaded into memory). The options are few. Pick a grid, a width and a feature below and the page shows the Python line you would write and what the grid really did with that feature when it was built and run for this page.

        

        

        
  
        OptionOnWhat it does
        
  
    
        widthbothBits per word, 1 to 64 (0, 65 and above are refused with “min_bit_width must be between 1 and 64”). Default 32. Every word in transit is cut to this many bits.
        
    
        merge_modeFlexGrid onlyWhat a relay that listens on several faces does with simultaneous words: "arbitrate" (default), "join-or", or a list such as "cell=join-or,arbitrate" (a mode per consuming cell, the last bare word is the default), or a dict. Anything else is refused: “unknown merge mode… use one of ['arbitrate', 'join-or']”.
        
    
        min_bit_width in the ICM file headerthe designThe width a design asks for. StepSim (and so the Composer) uses it when no width is given; with no flag the width is 32. Files wider than 64 or below 1 are refused on load.
        
    
        width in the Composer's sim requestComposer serverThe server accepts a width in the “start” request (nano/composer_page_v1.py line 129), but the Start button on the page does not send one, so in practice the design's own flag decides.
        
    
        --width / -w on the assemblerthe build, not the VMThat is the width of the Verilog the assembler writes. It is separate from the VM's width; see the Assembler tab for its flags and rules, and the MAN File tab for how a card's native width comes into it.
        
          

        


        3. The same design on both grids
        

        Each experiment is a few cells with the same words injected on the same ticks into each grid. Click one, then read the cards. Gold-edged cards are SuperGrid, green-edged cards are FlexGrid. A chip such as tick 3 → 1 means the output cell held the value 1 after tick 3.
        

        

        

        

        

        


        4. What each grid will accept
        

        Each row is a feature built on its own at each width, on each grid. Rows that need a running word (the add-ons) were fed a word and ticked a few times, because the standard grid only objects when the add-on is used. Click any square to read the message the grid gave.
        

        acceptedaccepted with a warningrefusednot an option there
        

        

        Click a square.
        

        Reading it: the standard grid's honest range is 32 bits. At any other width it still moves words and adds, but refuses add-ons and the nano gate, and warns for the accumulator, branch and priority cores because no one has checked those against hardware at other widths. FlexGrid exists to be right at other widths: the flex cells are built with a width, so it accepts the add-ons (as wiring), the nano gates the flex generator knows (12 topologies), and the cores that were checked against the real flex Verilog at widths 4 to 36.
        


        5. Handing either grid to a session
        

        VMSession is the driver port the Workbench and scripts use. It does not care which grid it is given. This was run for this page, with the library adder at 18 bits:
        

        import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "nano"); sys.path.insert(0, "tools")
import icm_v3
from flex_grid_v1 import FlexGrid
from vm_ai_port_v1 import VMSession

icm = icm_v3.IcmV3File.load("nano/library_std/add.icm.json")
s = VMSession(FlexGrid(icm.records, width=18))
s.inject(2, 1, 7); s.inject(6, 1, 5)       # the a and b input cells
print(s.run_to_quiescence())               # ticks until nothing moves
print(s.describe_cell(4, 14)["ram"]["data_reg"])   # the r output cell
        

        

        That is the route a later Workbench or mirror page would take to offer a flex variant: the session already accepts it; what is missing is the choice in those tools.
        


        6. How far to trust this page
        

          
  
        • Python only. These runs are the Python VM. Whether FlexGrid matches the Verilog is claimed in nano/flex_grid_v1.py and in the ledger (cell by cell, at widths 4 to 36, plus ten designs on the board); this page did not repeat it, and no Verilog simulator was available when it was built.
          • 
  
        • Small designs. Each experiment has three to five cells so the difference is visible. They are not library designs, except the width experiment, which is the 27-cell library adder.
          • 
  
        • Found while writing it. (1) At 32 bits the standard grid gave an unshifted word, with no error, for a coarse shift amount of 3 that is not one of its taps; the add-on chain defines taps at 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 and 28 only. (2) _ALLOWS_CARRY_MODE is set on both classes and read by nothing; the carry word works on both grids, so that flag is leftover. Both are reported, not fixed.
          • 
  
        • Not covered. The cross and corner tiles (FlexGrid replaces each with hidden register slices, one tick per tile; a one-tile test gave the same tick count on both), the ram hold mode, the sequencer, the priority arbiter and the GPU backend were not compared here.
          •

        The Mirror VM: Pretending to Be One Card
        The VM can be made to reflect a particular card: its layout, and (separately) its word width. The layout rule drawn live over real library designs, a simulated Walker you can step through, the two mirrors run together by hand, the options and every refusal, and what is not joined up yet.
        

        



        “Mirror” is the VM pretending to be one particular card. The MAN File tab described the card; the Assembler tab builds for it; the Two Grids tab showed the two versions of the VM's grid. This page is where those meet, and where they do not meet yet. Everything here was run on the real Python, on the two MAN files in the repository.
        


        1. Three things called mirror
        

        
  
        Free modeShape mirrorFlex mirror
        
  
    
        You make it withSuperGrid(records)VMSession.from_man(man, cells, ...)FlexGrid(records, width=18)
        
    
        GridSuperGridSuperGrid, width 32FlexGrid, any width
        
    
        What it copies from the cardnothingthe layout: which squares existthe behaviour: word width, handshake
        
    
        What it checksnothingevery cell sits on a square a real build would have; no two share a squarerefuses what the flex hardware cannot do (Two Grids tab)
        
    
        What it reads from the MAN file–only the card's id (and the cell count you give it)nothing: you give the width by hand
        
          

        

        Today these are separate. from_man builds a standard grid at 32 bits and checks the layout; the flex mirror is a width you type. Nothing reads the Tang's native width of 18 from its MAN file to start a FlexGrid. Section 5 runs both, by hand, together.
        


        2. The layout rule, and what it does to a design
        

        A card with n cells is laid out as a near-square block, filled row by row: rows = ⌈√n⌉, columns = ⌈n / rows⌉, the last row possibly short. It is the same pair of functions (grid_dims, cell_positions in the assembler) that the build uses, so the mirror cannot drift from it. Choose a card, a cell count and a design from the Composer's library. Green cells are where the design sits inside the layout; red are cells that sit on squares a real build of that size would not have.
        

        
  
  
  

        

        

        

        

        


        3. Fitting the shape is not fitting the chip
        

        The mirror asks “is each cell on a square the build would make”. It does not ask “would the chip hold that many squares”. The card-fit budgets answer the second question (quoted from the MAN tab, at the measured cost of one position):
        

        

        


        4. The Walker: finding out what is on the card
        

        A real card does not hand over its map. The plan (#501 in the ledger) is that a host program walks it: ask a cell “who are you”, or ask it to pass a question one step north, south, east or west, and note who answers. The Walker below is the simulated version, run against the mirrored VM of the library adder (27 cells) on the Tang's layout of 400 cells. It starts from one cell it is told about (the a input) and may only learn what a ping reveals. Press Step, or Play.
        

        

        

        

        

        What the Walker hands back (a SHAPE record)
        


        5. Both mirrors together, by hand
        

        The same adder, 200000 + 100000, run two ways. from_man gives the shape check and a 32-bit standard grid. Starting a FlexGrid at the width the Tang's MAN file declares gives the behaviour the chip would have. Doing both is a few lines; no tool does it for you yet. Real output:
        

        import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "nano"); sys.path.insert(0, "tools")
import icm_v3, vm_mirror_v1
from vm_ai_port_v1 import VMSession
from flex_grid_v1 import FlexGrid

man = "docs/man/tang-nano-20k.man.json"
icm = icm_v3.IcmV3File.load("nano/library_std/add.icm.json")

a = VMSession.from_man(man, 400, icm_path="nano/library_std/add.icm.json")   # shape check, SuperGrid at 32

bounds = vm_mirror_v1.load_mirror_bounds(man, 400)
assert not vm_mirror_v1.check_records_fit(icm.records, bounds)               # shape check, by hand
f = VMSession(FlexGrid(icm.records, width=18))                                # behaviour at the MAN's native width
f.mirror_bounds = bounds

Builds the layout, checks every cell of the program against it, then builds a SuperGrid. On success session.mirror_bounds holds the card id, rows and columns.

Every program loaded afterwards is checked. With a shell (an assembler shell version, v1 to v9) its core kinds are checked too.

        7. How far to trust this page
        

          
  
        • Shape only. The mirror checks positions, not chip capacity, speed or routing. Its own file header says so, and section 3 shows how far apart the two questions can be.
          • 
  
        • The MAN file barely matters. The mirror reads only the card id from it. Running every library design at ten cell counts on both cards gave identical fit results; only the card id in the message differed. The Tang and Mustang files differ in what the other tools read (the MAN File tab), not here.
          • 
  
        • The Walker is a simulation. It asks the VM, hop by hop, the questions the real protocol would ask a card, and never looks at the grid directly. The real mechanism it stands for (a discovery mode in the cell) is not built in hardware, and no real card has been walked.
          • 
  
        • Placement has to match the generator. A design placed as a long thin strip (the 32 by 184 fp16 adder) is refused at every cell count up to 400, even though it might be small in cells; the check follows the generator's near-square array, not the design's own bounding box.
          • 
  
        • Not built. A FlexGrid version of from_man and of the Workbench target, and anything that carries the MAN's native width into the VM. The Workbench builds a SuperGrid whatever target is set.
          • 
  
        • Python only. No Verilog was simulated for this page; unit tests not re-run.
          •

        Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§14 / 28
        The Workbench: See and Use the VM
        The workbench is where you sit at the VM: load a small program, deliver values into cells, step the clock and watch every register. A labelled screenshot, a worked 7 + 5, what it can and cannot show, and which grid it builds and what you can set.
        

        



        The workbench is the part of the VM you can sit at. You give it a small program, press a button, and watch every cell's registers change as the clock ticks. You can also push a value into any cell yourself. It is the quickest way to see the VM, the thing the previous page described, doing something.
        


        
  Open the workbench (once it is running)
  Workbench source
  The session behind it
  Design note

        

        The first link works only after you start the workbench on your own computer: run python3 nano/workbench_v1.py in the repository folder. It serves on port 7420 and opens your browser by itself (add a number after it for another port). Leave that terminal window open; closing it stops the workbench.
        


        1. The workbench, part by part
        

        This is a real screenshot, taken after loading the adder demo, delivering a 7 and a 5, adding a second small program as its own region, and pressing Step twice. Click a number on the picture, or a line in the list, to see where it is.
        


        

          


          2. A worked example: 7 + 5
          

          This is exactly what we did to get the screenshot, and what the cell showed at each point. The numbers are copied from the screen, not typed from memory.
          

            
  
          1. In Demos choose adder_pair and press Load as single program. The grid shows one cell, an adder at row 0, column 0. It sends its result east and takes its two inputs from the north and the west. Everything is zero or false and data_valid is false: nothing to offer yet.
            2. 
  
          2. In Execution set row 0, col 0, dir n, value 7 and press Deliver. The cell now shows a_reg: 7 and a_arrived: true. It has the first number and is waiting for the second.
            3. 
  
          3. Set dir w, value 5 and press Deliver again. The cell shows out_buffer: 12 and data_valid: true, and a_arrived has gone back to false. That is the answer, already waiting to be taken.
            4. 
  
          4. Press Step a few times. Nothing changes: out_buffer stays 12 and data_valid stays true. The adder points east, there is no cell to the east to take the 12, so it simply holds it. A value is never thrown away just because nobody has asked for it.
            5. 
  
          5. Now add a neighbour. Type program p2 { place r1 as ram_constant at (0,0) { out: e init_data: 42 } } into Program source, give it the region name answer_ram, clear both offset boxes and press Load as region. The workbench finds a free square by itself, (0, 1), right beside the adder, and the grid now shows a ram cell holding 42.
            6. 
  
          6. Under the button an amber hint appears: the adder sends east toward that ram cell, but the ram cell is not set up to listen from the west, so the 12 would never arrive. The workbench tells you, but it does not stop you, because in the VM a connection with nobody listening is not an error, only data that goes nowhere.
            7. 

          

          That hint is the useful lesson. Two cells being next to each other does not join them. Each cell has to be set to send on a face and the neighbour has to be set to listen on the opposite face. The workbench checks this for you; on the real chip nothing does.
          


          3. Everything is also a request
          

          Each button on the page just sends a request to the workbench's small web server, and the server passes it to the VM. So a script can do exactly what you did by hand. These are the calls behind the buttons you used above:
          

          requestwhat it does
          
  
          GET /stateEvery cell and its registers, as text a program can read.
          
  
          GET /demos, POST /load_demoList the ready-made programs; load one.
          
  
          POST /compileReplace everything with a new program (DSL or Python).
          
  
          POST /load_region, /clear_regionAdd a program as a named region, or remove just that region.
          
  
          POST /deliverPush a value into one cell from one side.
          
  
          POST /stepAdvance the clock by n ticks.
          
  
          POST /start_run, /pause_run, GET /run_statusAuto-play at a chosen rate, pause it, ask how far it got.
          
  
          POST /save_icm, /load_icm, /load_icm_regionWrite the grid to an ICM file, or read one back (as the whole grid or as a region).
          
  
          POST /set_target, /clear_target, GET /target, /shellsMake the grid a checked copy of a real card (below).
          

          

          For example curl -s -X POST localhost:7420/load_demo -d '{"name":"adder_pair"}', then two /deliver calls with value 7 from n and 5 from w, gave back the same cell state as the screen: out_buffer 12, data_valid true. The Save current grid to file button writes an ICM file, the same kind of file the Composer saves (see its page). For the single adder it holds one record: "core": "adder" at row 0, column 0, with upstream_mask ["n","w"] and downstream_mask ["e"], and it says "cell_type": "unicell_super_v1", the standard-mode cell, not a flex cell.
          


          4. The real target
          

          Normally the grid is free: any shape you like. The Real target box makes it a checked copy of a real card instead. You give it a card description (a MAN file; the box starts with docs/man/mustang-f100-a10.man.json), a number of cells and a "shell", which is the set of cell kinds that card's chip can actually contain. Pressing Set target with the box as it comes (4 cells, shell v3) gave a 2-by-2 grid for the card mustang-f100-a10-01 and the allowed kinds accumulator, adder, branch, comparator, latch, nano, ram and sequencer. After that, a program that asks for a cell the card cannot hold is refused. Clear target goes back to free mode.
          


          5. What it is, and what it is not
          

            
  
          • It runs the standard-mode VM (SuperGrid; section 6 below and the Two Grids tab). The cells on its grid are the standard ones, with fields such as downstream_mask and upstream_mask. They are not the flex cells from the earlier pages (branch with fixed and flowing inputs, priority, shift and so on). Designs for those are drawn and run in the Composer.
            • 
  
          • You give it programs written as text (the small DSL language, or Python through the Python front end), or ICM files. It has no drawing board. That is the Composer's job; the two are different tools that share the ICM file.
            • 
  
          • It shows registers, not a diagram. Each cell is a box of its fields. There are no wires drawn and no picture of data moving.
            • 
  
          • Seeing a value is not the same as it having moved. A cell like the adder holds its answer until a neighbour takes it, so an unchanging screen can mean "finished" or "stuck". The tick counter and the hint line help tell which.
            • 
  
          • Auto-play stops by itself when a tick produces no activity at all. An empty grid, for instance, ran for one tick and stopped.
            • 
  
          • Machine note: the workbench script keeps the terminal busy in a tight loop while it waits, so it will use one core of your computer fully until you stop it with Ctrl+C.
            • 

          


          6. Which grid it builds, and what you can set
          

          The Two Grids tab described the standard grid (SuperGrid) and the flex mirror (FlexGrid). The Workbench has no choice between them: every route that builds a grid (compile, load a demo, load an ICM file, load a region, set or clear a target, restore a saved state) makes a SuperGrid at 32 bits. The word FlexGrid does not appear anywhere in nano/workbench_v1.py. Pick a thing to do below; the result is what the Workbench really gave when each was run for this page, with the library adder and 200000 + 100000 (a sum that shows the word width: 300000 at 32 bits, 37856 at 18).
          

          

          

          What you can set when you start it
          

          SettingHowNote
          
  
          Portpython3 nano/workbench_v1.py 7420The only command-line option. Default 7420, served on localhost only, and it opens your browser itself.
          
  
          Card and cell countPOST /set_target (the Real target box)Checks layout against the card, as the Mirror VM tab shows. The grid it makes is still a SuperGrid. Details of the MAN file are on the MAN File tab.
          
  
          Shellshell in /set_targetWhich cell kinds the card's chip contains (shells v1 to v9, from the Mirror tab); programs using other kinds are refused.
          
  
          Auto-play speedticks_per_sec in /start_runDefault 1 tick a second.
          
  
          Word width–No setting. 32 bits. An ICM file that declares min_bit_width is loaded without error and the declaration is not used.
          
  
          Merge mode–No setting; that is a FlexGrid option.
          

          

          

          What it would take to offer a flex Workbench
          

          Not built. Reading the code and the runs above: the controller is a thin layer over VMSession, which accepts either grid; the six places that build a SuperGrid would need a choice (and a width, and a merge mode); /state shows cells and the tick count but not which grid or width it is, so the page could not tell you; and the page has no control for either. The same gap is in from_man, which the Workbench uses for targets (Mirror VM tab). Alan's plan is for both to come in the two variants; this page records where it stands.
          

          Data: docs/teaching/capture_wb_v1.py → wb_data.json, from the real controller and a real local HTTP server on a free port. Python VM only; Workbench unit tests not re-run; the live page was not re-checked for this section.

Your screen may lay out differently. The saved-file wording and the list of requests come from the source file's header and from running them; the unit tests for the workbench (tests/vm/test_workbench_v1.py) were not re-run for this page.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§15 / 28
          Programming: The DSL
          The small text language for placing cells and wiring their faces. Sketch a program and see it drawn, watch a real run (including a timing mistake that loses a number), see the compiler's own error messages, and meet the tiles.
          

          



          The DSL is the small text language for placing cells on the grid and wiring them to their neighbours. A program says which kind of cell goes on which square, and which faces it listens on and sends out of. The compiler checks that and writes an ICM file, the same kind of file the Composer saves. This page lets you sketch placements and see them drawn, shows what a real run of a DSL program looks like (including a mistake that is easy to make), and shows what the real compiler says when you slip.
          


          
  The DSL manual
  Compiler source
  Command line tool
  The tile library

          


          1. A program is a list of placements
          

          This program adds two numbers using four cells. Read it line by line:
          

          

            
  
          • program seven_plus_five { ... } is the wrapper: a file holds exactly one program, and its name becomes the name inside the saved file.
            • 
  
          • place x as ram_flowing at (0, 0) { ... } means: put a cell called x (a name for you and for error messages) that behaves as the ram_flowing tile, on row 0, column 0. A tile is a ready-made behaviour for a cell.
            • 
  
          • in: w and out: e are ports: this cell takes a value in from its west face and offers it out of its east face. Faces are the four compass points n s e w. Row numbers grow going south and column numbers going east, so square (0, 1) is just east of (0, 0).
            • 
  
          • The adder at (0, 1) listens on west (where x offers its value) and south (where y, one row below it, offers its value upward). It sends its answer east to sink.
            • 
  
          • Some fields are parameters, not ports: a number the tile needs, like init_data: 7 on a constant.
            • 

          

          Cells are joined only by facing each other: one sends out of its east face and the neighbour to its east listens on its west face. There are no wires to draw.
          


          2. Sketch your own
          

          Edit the program and the picture follows. This is a sketch drawn by this page's own script: it knows the fourteen basic tiles (below), draws their ports, and tells you when two neighbours do not face each other. It does not compile anything. The real compiler's wording is in section 4.
          

          Start from:
  
  
  
  
          


          

          


          3. Timing is your job
          

          Here is that 7 + 5 program running in the VM. We put a 7 into x and a 5 into y, and let the clock tick. The table shows the adder and the sink after each tick. The numbers are copied from a real run.
          

          Inject the 5:
  
  
          

          tickwhat we didadder a_rega_arrivedadder out_buffersink value
          

          

          So the DSL does exactly what you wrote, and nothing more: it does not arrange for the two operands to reach the adder at different moments. In the same-tick run the adder holds one operand and waits for a second, and the second never counted. (The manual says the adder's two inputs share one field and whichever arrives first becomes A; that run fits it.) Making the arrival order certain is the programmer's job in the DSL. When programs are compiled from LLVM IR (next page) the compiler adds the ordering cells for you.
          


          4. What the compiler says when you slip
          

          These are five real mistakes, run through the real command line tool. Each message says where, what the problem is, and why. Pick one:
          

          

          The program
          

          What the compiler printed
          


          5. The tiles
          

          A tile is a behaviour you can put on a cell. These fourteen are the basic ones, read from the library itself. Every port is a face you wire; every parameter is a number you set.
          

          tileportsparameterswhat it does
          

          The compiler also knows tiles built out of several cells. sentinel is one: it watches a running count and raises a flag at a threshold. Placing it takes one statement:
          

          

          

          Besides the basic fourteen, the compiler accepts these names: . You can also make your own multi-cell tile inside a program with define and expose; the manual covers that.
          


          6. The same program in Python syntax
          

          The DSL is a text format of its own. There is a second front end that reads a declarative piece of ordinary Python syntax and produces the same thing:
          

          DSL
          Python syntax
          

          

          The Python is only read, never run: there are no loops, variables or arithmetic, just place(...) calls with literal values.
          


          7. What the DSL is not
          

            
  
          • It does not do the placing. The row and column numbers you write are used as they are. It is a way to write a shape down, not a tool that finds good squares.
            • 
  
          • It targets the standard-mode cells. Its tiles are the standard ones (ram, adder, accumulator and so on), the ones the Workbench shows. The flex family is reached by saving an ICM file and giving that to the assembler; the next page shows the route for a program that came from LLVM IR.
            • 
  
          • It does not draw. The Composer is the picture-based way to make the same kind of file.
            • 
  
          • One program per file. And a program with two placements on one square is refused (section 4).
            • 

          

          The tile table, the five error messages, the 7 + 5 run, the sentinel's three cells and the DSL/Python comparison were all produced by docs/teaching/capture_programming_v1.py running the real compiler and VM on 11 October 2026, and are embedded in this page; re-run that script to refresh them. The sketch in section 2 is this page's own JavaScript and is deliberately simpler than the compiler. The compiler's unit tests (tests/vm/test_dsl_compiler_v1.py) were not re-run for this page.
