          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§16 / 28
          Programming: From LLVM IR
          Take a real function as LLVM IR through the real compiler: see the cells it becomes, run them in the VM, see what it refuses, and follow the route on to the flex family's Verilog.
          

          



          LLVM IR is the plain-text form that many compilers (the one behind C, C++ and Rust among them) write out just before they produce machine code. It looks like assembly for an imaginary tidy processor: every step is one small named operation. UniCell can take that text and turn it into a design of cells, so a function written in an ordinary language can, in principle, become something this machine runs. This page takes real functions through the real compiler, shows what comes out, and is honest about what it refuses.
          


          
  The compiler (source)
  Command line tool
  Route to the flex family
  The earlier front end

          

          To try it yourself, save a function as f.ll and run python3 nano/llvm_cli_v1.py f.ll -o f.icm. It needs the llvmlite package (pip install llvmlite). We have no C compiler in this session, so the functions below are written directly as LLVM IR; the result for a C function is the same kind of file.
          


          1. A function becomes cells
          

          Pick an example. On the left is the IR text. On the right is the grid of cells the compiler produced, one square per cell, coloured by the job the cell does. Hover a square to see its name. Everything shown here is the real compiler's output.
          

          

          
  
          LLVM IR
          
  
          The cells
          
    
          
    
          

          

          

          


          2. Does it give the right answer?
          

          Each row below is a real run: the compiled cells were loaded into the VM, the inputs were put in, the clock ran, and the answer was read from the result cell. The last columns compare it with plain arithmetic done in Python. Results are 32-bit numbers, so a negative answer shows as a large positive one (for example -3 is 4294967293).
          

          

          


          3. What the cell roles are
          

          A function with three operations did not become three cells. Using the first example, the compiler's job was to turn each line into a working cell and to make sure the right numbers reach it in the right order:
          

            
  
          • Compute cells are the arithmetic: one adder or multiplier for each add or mul line. The sub %p, 3 line became an adder that adds 0xFFFFFFFD (that is, -3), which is cheaper: the compiler's own note says so.
            • 
  
          • Argument and constant cells hold the inputs and the literal numbers until they are used.
            • 
  
          • Ordering cells (priority cells) sit in front of an arithmetic cell and let its two operands in one at a time instead of racing. As the DSL page showed, two operands arriving on the same tick can lose one. The compiler puts one in front of every two-operand operation, so the answer does not depend on how long each route turned out to be.
            • 
  
          • Relay cells carry a number along a path across the grid, one square per tick, because cells only talk to their immediate neighbours.
            • 

          

          So the clever part of the compiler is not the arithmetic. It is the plumbing: placing cells, routing relays between them, and controlling how arrivals are let in so that nothing is lost the way it was in the DSL page's second run.
          


          4. Choices and loops
          

          There are no jumps on this machine: every cell that exists works whenever data reaches it. So the compiler turns the usual control-flow ideas into dataflow:
          

            
  
          • An if becomes a select. Choose "A choice" above: the larger of two numbers. Both branches are always computed and a select picks one, built out of smaller operations (a subtract and compare, then masks with and, xor and or). The compiler listed exactly that for it. That is why a tiny function came to 66 cells.
            • 
  
          • A loop is unrolled. Choose "A loop that runs four times": the body is copied four times, one after another, and the loop counter disappears. That needs the number of times round the loop to be known when compiling. The limits in the source are 64 repeats and 600 instructions after unrolling.
            • 

          

          And these are real refusals, the compiler's own words:
          

          

          

          The compiler's own caveat on the comparison used above is worth reading too: 
          


          5. Which operations it knows
          

          LLVM operationWhat it becomes
          
  
          add, sub, mulAn adder, a subtractor (as an add of the negated constant where it can), a multiplier.
          
  
          and, or, xorA bitwise gate cell.
          
  
          shl, lshrA shift, with the amount a literal number written in the code (shown above as "one-operand shl with amount 2").
          
  
          icmp, select, br, phiSmaller operations put together, as in the max example: both sides are computed, then one is picked.
          
  
          ashr, zext, sext, truncThe source lists these as expandable into the operations above. We did not run them for this page.
          
  
          anything else, such as sdivRefused, with a message (section 4). The source says an escalation scheme for new operations (look in a shared library, then research, then build it in the Composer) is planned and not built.
          

          

          All of it works on 32-bit integers (i32).
          


          6. On to the flex family
          

          The compiler writes an ICM file for the standard-mode cells. The flex family (the Tang Nano 20K's cells) is reached by two more steps, and we ran them on the first example:
          

          

          

          The assembler's report says it made 17 cells with 3 joins from a 20-cell file: the three ordering cells are not cells any more in the flex version. There the cells hand data on with a ready and acknowledge handshake, so the order can be arranged by the wiring itself. The files written are the Verilog for the three kinds of cell used (adder, multiplier, ram) and a top file that connects them.
          

          We generated this Verilog but did not simulate it here: the Verilog simulator is not installed in this session. The project's README says the 41 test programs compiled this way were each run as generated Verilog and matched the VM and plain arithmetic; that is quoted, not re-checked now.
          


          7. What this is not
          

            
  
          • It is not a general compiler. One function, whole numbers only, a fixed list of operations, loops only when the count is known when compiling. Anything else is refused with a reason, never silently wrong, with the one exception the compiler itself warns about: the signed comparison can give a wrong answer when the two numbers are very large and of opposite sign.
            • 
  
          • Arguments are runtime inputs. The same compiled cells give the right answer for any inputs, as the runs above show, because each argument is a cell you load with a value.
            • 
  
          • An earlier front end still exists. llvm_ir_frontend_v1.py compiles a restricted counting loop onto a small ring of four cells instead of unrolling it. The command line tool used here is the newer one.
            • 
  
          • The VM runs it; the chip has run only smaller things. The README lists designs run live on the Tang board (a CORDIC, a relay, a reduction tree). We have not run these examples on the board.
            • 

          

          Every cell position, count, run result, rewrite note, caveat and refusal on this page was produced by docs/teaching/capture_programming_v1.py running the real compiler (llvm_dag_frontend_v1.py) and the VM on 11 October 2026 and is embedded here. The route-to-flex numbers come from the same script running llvm_cli_v1.py, flexsub_compile_v1.py and project_assemble_v1.py. The compiler's unit tests were not re-run for this page.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§17 / 28
          The Compiler: From Description to Cells
          One real function followed through the compiler's five stages, the two ways in, how it reports every problem at once, how it decides what lets two values into a cell, the operations it has, and whether the result fits a card.
          

          



          The compiler is the part that turns a description of what you want into cells placed on a grid, with their faces set so they join up, saved as an ICM file. This page follows one real function through it stage by stage, shows how the two ways in (the DSL and LLVM IR) differ, how it reports problems, how it decides what goes in front of an adder, which operations it has, and whether the result fits a real card. The next page covers the placing and tightening in more depth.
          


          
  LLVM front end
  DSL back end
  Growth placer
  Routed placer
  Decision rule
  Card fit

          


          1. One function, five stages
          

          This is the function from the LLVM IR page. Click a stage to see what went in and what came out. Every box of text is the compiler's own output.
          

          

          

          


          2. Two ways in, and what they share
          

          There are two front doors and they do not share all their insides. What they share is the result: a list of cells in an ICM file.
          

            
  
          • The DSL (and the Python-syntax reader) go through a small description called ProgramIR: a program name and a list of placements, each with a tile, a square and some fields. Then one shared back end checks each placement against the tile's own rules, places it and writes the records. Here is the 7 + 5 program from the DSL page as the compiler sees it:
            • 

          

          After reading the text: 
          

          The placements (ProgramIR)
          nametilerowcolfields
          

            
  
          • LLVM IR goes a different way. The front end keeps the real dataflow (which value feeds which operation), because a ProgramIR already contains squares, and recovering the dataflow from squares would mean working backwards from geometry. So it builds a list of operations, hands that to a placer, and the placer decides every square itself. The comments in the source say exactly this.
            • 

          

          So a DSL program puts the squares in your hands, and an LLVM program leaves them to the compiler.
          


          3. It tells you everything wrong at once
          

          A compiler that stops at the first mistake makes you fix and re-run again and again. This one collects every independent problem. Here is a DSL file with three separate mistakes and what the real tool printed:
          

          

          The LLVM front end is different at its first step, because the real LLVM parser it uses (llvmlite) stops at the first thing it rejects. Here is a function with two undefined names and what came back:
          

          

          Only the first undefined name, %q, is reported. The later stages (resolve, check) do collect all their own problems; this parser step does not.
          


          4. How two values are let in: the decision rule
          

          The DSL page showed an adder losing a number when both arrived together. When the compiler builds a design, it has to put something in front of every cell that takes two values, and which thing depends on three questions. Answer them and the real rule gives its choice:
          

          
  
  
  

          

          

          These answers come straight from the compiler's own function, run for all eight combinations. In practice the routed placer, which is the usual one, always puts a priority cell in front of a commutative operation and a sequencer in front of a non-commutative one, whatever it could have worked out, so that correctness never depends on how long a route happened to come out. The price is one extra cell per two-operand operation. A subtract of a constant avoids even that: x - 3 becomes x + (-3), which is commutative.
          


          5. The operations it knows
          

          operationtilecoreswap-safe?operands
          

          That is the whole library: eleven entries, read from the code. The LLVM names icmp and select are not in it; the compiler builds them from these (a compare is a subtract and a compare-against-threshold, a select is a subtract, an xor, two ands and an or), as the LLVM page showed. A shift is a "ram_flowing" cell with an amount set in its add-on field.
          


          6. Does it fit the card?
          

          All of the above produces a layout of some size. A real card has a fixed grid and a budget of cells. The compiler can be given a card description and refuses a design that does not fit. We asked it to fit the same function onto square grids of several sizes on the Mustang F100 card's description (budget  positions):
          

          gridresultthe compiler's report
          

          One thing we did not get to the bottom of: the layout is 7 rows by 8 columns, yet an 8 by 8 grid was refused and a 9 by 9 accepted. The refusal says no layout fits at any fold width. We did not investigate whether the grid needs a margin or something else is going on. Also, the report says the multiply "fell back to logic" because no free DSP block was found, which means this build uses the slower logic multiplier rather than a hard one. And these are limits the compiler states itself: the card's die coordinates are mapped onto the logical grid by an assumed mapping, because no post-fit data exists yet to fix it.
          


          7. What this is not
          

            
  
          • It is not an optimiser. The placing and routing are step-by-step heuristics, not a search for the best answer; the next page shows a case where a hand-chosen setting beat the default.
            • 
  
          • It does not verify itself. The runs on these pages compare the compiled cells against plain arithmetic for a handful of inputs. That is a check, not a proof.
            • 
  
          • It stops at the ICM file. Turning an ICM file into something a particular chip runs is the assembler's job (see the LLVM page's last section).
            •

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§18 / 28
          The Placer and the Tightener
          Putting cells on squares and joining them with relays, then making the result small and still correct: two placers side by side, tightening by spacing, folding, and the rat's-nest way of shrinking one connection a step at a time.
          

          



          Cells only talk to their immediate neighbours, so a design is not finished when every operation has a cell: the cells must also be put on squares and joined by relay cells so that values travel from where they are made to where they are used. That job is the placer. Making the result small and still correct is the tightener. This page shows both on real compiles: two placers side by side, tightening by spacing, folding into bands, and the "rat's nest" way of shrinking one connection step by step.
          


          
  Routed placer
  Growth placer
  Rat's-nest router
  Tightener
  Placer lessons

          


          1. Why placing is hard
          

            
  
          • A value moves one square per tick, and only to a neighbour. Two cells far apart need a chain of relay cells between them, and each relay is a cell you pay for.
            • 
  
          • No diagonals, and a relay can only go straight (the router's own notes record this). A route can turn only where a cell is set to turn it.
            • 
  
          • Routes must not cross. Two chains that meet on one square would be one chain. There is a cross tile (see the Routing page) but the placers described here do not use it, so a design that cannot be drawn without crossing is refused loudly rather than miscompiled.
            • 
  
          • A cell has four faces. A producer has three output faces, so one value can feed at most three consumers.
            • 

          


          2. Two placers, side by side
          

          The compiler has two placers. The growth placer builds the design outward from where the previous operation ended, adding a few padding cells before the next shape. The routed placer first arranges the operations in columns on a virtual canvas, then routes every connection across the whole canvas at once, and only then turns it into cells. The default, auto, compiles with both and keeps the smaller. Pick a function:
          

          

          
  
          Growth placer
          
  
          Routed placer
          

          

          

          

          Both give the right answer in the VM for the inputs we tried; they differ in size. The source comments give one more data point we did not re-measure: a five-times unrolled loop was 739 cells under growth and 140 routed, which matters because simulation time grows with the cell count.
          


          3. Tightening by spacing
          

          The routed placer spaces its operations apart on the canvas by a number, the spacing. Wide spacing makes routing easy and the design large; narrow spacing makes it small and may make routing fail. So it tightens: it tries the smallest spacing that works. Drag the slider to see the sum, product and subtract function from the first example laid out at each spacing, from our runs:
          

          

          

          

          


          4. Folding to fit a bounded card
          

          A long design is wide. A card is a fixed square. Folding wraps the columns into stacked bands, like a snake, so the design is tall and narrow instead. It costs extra cells (the turns need relays). The same function, folded to a given number of columns per band:
          

          

          

          

          Folding to 4 or more columns changed nothing here because the design was already narrow enough. The Compiler page showed which grid sizes the whole fit check accepted for this function.
          


          5. The rat's nest: loose first, then shrink
          

          An older and simpler idea, from Alan: place things loosely with plenty of room so it is easy to get right, see where routes meet (the nexus points, such as a priority cell where two values converge), then pull each connection in toward its nexus one step at a time, checking after every step that nothing broke, and stop the moment a step would. Here is one real connection. A value starts far away at the top left and has to reach a combine unit (a priority cell feeding an adder):
          

          

          

          the value (a ram cell holding 10)relay cellspriority cell (the nexus)adder
          

          


          6. What the placers have taught us
          

          The flex side has its own layout engine and the project keeps a file of what each design taught it. A few of those lessons, in plain words (the file has all of them):
          

            
  
          • Make a subtract order-free. A subtract is the common two-operand operation where operand order matters, and when the minuend's route is the long one the balancer cannot fix it. Rewriting a - b as a + (-1) * b removes the problem at the cost of a multiplier. The file marks this rule as done by hand in one engine and not yet automatic in the placer.
            • 
  
          • Route the shortest, most constrained lane first, while both ends are still open.
            • 
  
          • Leave room at the doors. Pin entries and exits to the edge of a tile and put a one-relay stub on each open face before routing, or earlier lanes wall the pin in.
            • 
  
          • A cell that makes two words is two lanes. A carry or high word leaving by its own faces has to be laid like a second output.
            • 
  
          • Retry with seeds. A placement that cannot route is undone and tried again in a different order.
            • 

          


          7. Limits, stated by the code itself
          

            
  
          • Routing is a sequence of heuristics, not an optimum. Shortest-first, then seeded reorderings, then more spacing. The source notes that routing under non-crossing constraints is a hard problem in general, which is why the Composer exists as a human fallback.
            • 
  
          • A design that cannot be laid out without crossings fails loudly. It does not produce a wrong answer.
            • 
  
          • The default tightener does not try every spacing. It tries 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 12 in that order and keeps the first that routes. In our run, asking for spacing 2 directly gave a smaller layout (18 cells in 5 by 6, against 20 in 7 by 8) that also gave the right answer for the inputs we tried. We did not run it further, so we cannot say 2 is always safe.
            • 
  
          • The rat's-nest tightener is narrow. It shrinks a free-moving value toward a fixed target. Its source says shrinking a connection between two fixed meeting points, where moving one end means re-routing everything on it, was a harder problem addressed later (there is a separate routine for a combine unit), and we have not shown that one here.
            • 
  
          • It is tested on small designs. The test for the rat's nest says a four-input reduction tree went from 186 loose cells to 90 and still computed correctly; that is quoted from the test file's description and was not re-run.
            • 

          

          All layouts, counts, answers and the tightening steps on this page were produced by docs/teaching/capture_compiler_v1.py running the real placers and tightener on 11 October 2026 and embedded here. The lessons in section 6 are paraphrased from docs/placer_lessons.md. The placers' unit tests were not re-run for this page.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§19 / 28
          Writing a Formula in LaTeX, and Writing It Small
          The compiler accepts an integer formula written as in a maths book, checks the design it builds against plain Python, and refuses what it cannot do with a message pointing at the character. How to write each kind of input (formulas, powers, division, sums and products, dot products, matrices), what is refused, and the reduction advisory: measured pairs showing how writing the same formula smaller changes the cell count.
          Writing a formula for UniCell: the LaTeX input and the reduction advisory
          

          You can hand the compiler a formula the way you would write it in a maths book (LaTeX), and it gives you back a design made of cells, after checking that the design gives the same answers as a plain Python evaluation of your formula. If the check fails you get an error and no design. This page says how to write each kind of input, what the compiler will say no to, and how to write a formula so that it comes out small.
          

          Every cell count below comes from a real run of nano/latex_cli_v1.py (12 October 2026). Counts are cells, not speeds: nothing here is a clock-rate claim. The designs were checked in the VM; the matrix, polynomial and division forms were also run as generated Verilog (flex family, and for some sub family) in earlier checks, listed in the ledger (#1066 to #1083).
          

          1. How to run it
          

          python3 nano/latex_cli_v1.py "y = (a + b)^2 - 3c" --set a=2 --set b=3 --set c=4 -o poly.icm

          

          Quote the formula. --set also runs the finished design on the values you give and prints the answer next to Python's. In code, the same thing is compile_latex(...) and, for matrices, compile_matrix_latex(...) in nano/latex_frontend_v1.py.
          

          2. How to write each kind of input
          

          Numbers and names. Whole numbers only. One letter is one variable (x). Two letters side by side are a product, as in maths: xy is x times y. For a longer name write \mathrm{rate}. Subscripts work: x_1, x_{12}. Greek letters work. The inputs of the design are the names in the formula, in the order they first appear; the CLI prints that order.
          

          Arithmetic. +  -  *  \cdot  \times, unary minus, and writing things side by side (2x, 3(a+b)). Brackets ( ) [ ] { } and \left( \right).
          

          Powers. Whole numbers 0 to 64. LaTeX takes only one digit after ^ unless you use braces, so write x^{23}, not x^23 (the compiler refuses the second, because in LaTeX it means x squared followed by a 3).
          

          Numbers wrap around. Arithmetic is on 32-bit whole numbers that wrap, exactly like the cells: 2^31 + 2^31 is 0. There are no fractions.
          

          Division and remainder. a / b, a \div b, \frac{a}{b} give the whole-number quotient (rounded down); a \bmod b gives the remainder. They work on unsigned words, so -x / 2 is not minus half of x. Dividing by zero gives all ones, and the remainder by zero is the dividend. By default one division is one cell (the division core); a / 7 and a \bmod 7 each came out at 8 cells in all. A divisor that is a power of two is a shift or a mask and costs a cell or two. The old written-out form (about 23,000 cells for one division) is still available as --division unrolled. Speed against size of the division cell is --div-steps K (K quotient bits per clock). K changes how big the cell physically is, so it is chosen when the design is built, not changed afterwards.
          

          Sums and products over a range. \sum_{i=1}^{4} i x and \prod_{i=1}^{3} (x+i). The first and last values must be whole numbers written out (at most 64 terms); \sum_{i=1}^{n} is refused because a range that depends on a run-time value needs a loop, which is not built. The index i can stand alone, be a subscript (a_i) or be an exponent (x^i). The body is the multiplicative term that follows, so \sum_{i=1}^{3} i x + 1 means (1+2+3)x + 1; put brackets round the body to include several terms.
          

          Dot products. Write the sum with subscripts: \sum_{i=1}^{3} a_i b_i. The inputs are named a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, a_3, b_3. A dot product of n terms is placed as a stored block (section 4) and is exactly 7n - 1 cells: 3 terms came out at 20.
          

          Matrices. Give a rule for the entries and a size, counting rows and columns from 1:
          

          python3 nano/latex_cli_v1.py "A_{ij} = i j" --matrix 3x3

          

          This builds y = A x: the inputs are x_1 ... x_n, the results are y_1 ... y_m. The rule is an ordinary formula in the two index letters, so i + j, i j, i^2 j^2, division and remainder all work. The entries are worked out when the design is built and become constant cells, so the rule may use only the two index letters. The 3 by 3 above came out at 68 cells and gave 14, 28, 42 for x = 1, 2, 3, as Python does. Sizes are 1 to 16 rows and 2 to 16 columns.
          

            

          • Run-time matrix: leave the rule off and every entry is an input: "A_{ij}" --matrix 2x3 gives inputs A_1_1 ... A_2_3 as well as x_1 ... x_3 (44 cells). Use this when the matrix itself is the result of another design.
            • 

          • Chaining, y = B (A x): add --then "B_{ij} = i j @ 2x2" (repeatable). Each next matrix needs as many columns as the one before has rows. A 2 by 3 followed by a 2 by 2 came out at 73 cells.
            • 

          • Matrix times matrix: done by streaming. The columns of the second matrix are fed one after another through one block of the first, so the hardware is one block, not one copy per column. For 16 by 16 that is about 2,000 cells against about 32,000 for a copy per column (worked out from the cell-count formula, not built).
            • 

          • Not built yet: the looped small form (one block reused by feeding its results back in), matrix entries that depend on a run-time value, matrices written out number by number, and a matrix with a single column.
            • 

          

          3. What it refuses, and what the refusal looks like
          

          The compiler never guesses. It points at the character and says why:
          

          


          
You wrote
What it says

          
          


          
y = x^23
write x^{23} with braces: in LaTeX x^23 means x^2 followed by 3

          

          
y = \sqrt{x}
square roots are not supported (no fractions or irrational results; only whole numbers)

          

          
y = a / b c
a number or name straight after a division or remainder is ambiguous (is it multiplied before or after?): add brackets

          

          
y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} i
the last value of a sum or product must be a whole number written out (a run-time range needs a loop, which is not built)

          

          
y = x^{-1}
negative powers mean division, which is not supported

          
          

          

          Also refused: functions (sin, log), integrals, decimals, variable exponents, absolute value, comparisons, shifts, and anything it does not recognise.
          

          4. The reduction advisory: write the smaller formula yourself
          

          The system does not reduce your formula for you. It does only small clean-ups: constants are folded, x + 0 and x * 1 are removed, a one-variable polynomial is expanded and rebuilt as the cheaper of two shapes (below), and a pure dot product is placed as a stored block. Anything bigger, such as factoring, pulling a constant out of a sum, or noticing that two terms are the same, is up to whoever writes the formula. This follows Alan's reading: the user supplies the reduced formula, or a reduction step runs first, and that second route may be too much of an extension of the LaTeX input, so it is not built. The pairs below show how much a hand reduction gains.
          

          The advice below is each time a measured pair. The only thing that changed between the two is how the formula is written.
          

          Pull constants and common factors out.
          

          


          
Written
Cells

          
          


          
\sum_{i=1}^{8} i x
284

          

          
36 x (the same value)
8

          

          
a b + a c + a d + a e
89

          

          
a (b + c + d + e)
26

          
          

          

          The reason is the cost of reading the same input more than once. Every extra read of an input needs a split, and the general placer pays for the wires with relay cells (a relay is a cell that only carries a value). A formula that uses one input many times is expensive, and the cost grows faster than the number of terms. Factor first.
          

          Polynomials: the compiler tries two shapes and keeps the smaller. A polynomial in one variable is built as written ("direct") and as Horner (((c3 x + c2) x + c1) x + c0, one multiply-add stage per degree), and the one with fewer cells is kept. You can force one with --polynomial horner or direct. Measured: 3x^2 + 2x + 1 is 26 cells (44 direct); x^7 is 38 (61 direct); but (x+1)^3 is 23 direct and 32 by Horner, so direct is kept. A dense polynomial costs exactly 12 cells per degree plus 2. The choice is made on compiled cells, not on counting multiplies, because fewer multiplies did not always mean fewer cells (x^7 needs more multiplies by Horner and still comes out smaller). Two ways of writing the same polynomial can land on the same size: x^2 (x+1)^2 and x^4 + 2x^3 + x^2 both came out at 32 cells.
          

          A sum is a chain, not a tree. Adding n things one after another costs 6 cells per term; a balanced tree of adds, which looks better on paper, was far larger (8 terms: 101 cells against 44). The compiler writes ranges out as a chain, so you do not need to arrange this yourself. The cause of the tree being worse has not been found.
          

          Dot products and matrices go to a stored block. The general placer routes a dot product badly: 2 to 9 terms cost 29, 53, 89, 137, 188, 260, 326, 413 cells, mostly relay cells. The stored multiply-accumulate block is written directly and is exactly 7n - 1 cells (8 terms: 55). A matrix times a vector is the same idea laid side by side, with 8n(m-1) + 7n - 1 cells for m rows and n columns (2 by 2: 29, 3 by 3: 68, 4 by 4: 123). So: write a dot product as a bare \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i and a matrix as a rule plus a size, and the compiler uses the block. Add a coefficient, repeat a variable or use a subtraction inside the dot product and it quietly falls back to the general placer and the larger design (--blocks off forces that on purpose).
          

          Check the count, then decide. The CLI prints compiled: N cells. Rewriting a formula and running it again takes seconds, and the count is the measurement. A card limits how many cells fit, and the card-fit check refuses a design that is too big.
          

          5. How far it goes, and what has and has not been checked
          

            

          • Checked: every compile compares the design with Python on corner values (0, 1, the sign boundary, all ones) and random values, once on the generated operations and once in the VM. Division, polynomials, sums, products, dot products and matrices were also run as generated flex Verilog in iverilog; division, a dot product and a 1 by 3 matrix were run as sub Verilog.
            • 

          • Not checked: the LaTeX designs on the older v4/v4c carrier cells; anything on a physical card; throughput when items are fed close together (the streaming helper uses a deliberately generous gap, a rule of thumb and not a measured limit); sizes of matrices beyond the small ones in RTL.
            • 

          • Not built: loops (sums or matrix products over a run-time range), signed division, fractions and fixed point, comparisons and choices, shifts written in LaTeX.
            •

          The Verilog, and Keeping the Program Apart from the Card
          The hardware form of the design: one short file per kind of cell, in two families, and how the program (a card-neutral map) is kept separate from the card (the MAN file) until a tool combines them. Try the same program against two real cards.
          

          



          Verilog is the language the hardware is written in. Everything on earlier pages ran in the VM, a Python model of the cells. This page is about the other form of the same design: a small text file per kind of cell, which a chip tool turns into real wiring inside an FPGA (a chip you can rewire). It also shows where the design keeps what the program does apart from which card it runs on.
          


          What is in the Verilog folder
          

          Everything lives in sub/verilog/. Each kind of cell is one short file, and each has a matching test file (a "testbench") that feeds it numbers and checks what comes out. The counts below are read from the folder when this page was built.
          

          

          Two families exist side by side. The stripped family (v4s) has no way for a cell to say "wait": every cell takes a fixed number of clock ticks, so the builder must pad early paths with spare relay cells so values meet on the same tick. The flex family (v4sa) adds a "ready / taken" handshake and a word width you choose, so cells wait for each other and nothing needs padding. Pick a family to see the cells it has and the real ports of its adder.
          

          

          

          

          


          Where the design keeps the logic apart from the card
          

          A program is written once, as a map of cells (an ICM file). It says nothing about any card: no pins, no chip sizes, no clock. What the card offers is held in a second file, the MAN file (the next page). A tool called the assembler reads both and writes the Verilog and the build script for that pairing. Change the card file and the same program is built differently; change the program and the same card is used differently.
          

          

          In the docs these are four named things (docs/man/README.md):
          

          
  
          ArtifactWhat it holdsChanges whenUsed on this page
          
  
          ICMthe user's program as cells and wiring; the same file for every cardthe program changesyes, add and mul
          
  
          MANone card's identity and abilities: chip size, multipliers, pins, which options its tools accepta different card, rarelyyes, two cards
          
  
          SHAPEone compiled design's own layoutevery buildno
          
  
          BITSTREAMSHAPE and MAN together, turned into what is loaded on the chipevery buildno
          

          

          The MAN file in detail →

The left card is the Sipeed Tang Nano 20K (a small Gowin FPGA, the project's active line). The right card is the IEI Mustang-F100-A10 (an Intel Arria 10 card, the older reference line). Anything that differs between the two columns is marked.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§21 / 28
          The MAN File: One Card, Written Down
          What is inside a card file, who reads each part (the assembler, the mirror VM and the card-fit check), what a cell costs on the card, what the card claims it can do, and how far each of the two real files can be trusted.
          

          



          The MAN file is one card, written down. It holds what the card is (the chip, how big it is, what built-in blocks it has, which legs carry the clock and the lights) and what its tools accept. It holds nothing about any program. The previous page showed the assembler reading it; this page opens the files themselves.
          


          Two real files
          

          

          Both live in docs/man/. They differ in age and in how they were made, and that shows in what they contain. Which fields a card file has decides what the tools can do for that card; where a field is missing, the tools fall back or refuse.
          


          Open a file
          

          

          Each row is a top-level section of the file; the bar is its size in the file. Click one for what it is for and what in the repository reads it.
          

          

          


          Who uses the MAN file
          

          Three things read a card file today, and they read very different amounts of it.
          

          
  
          UserWhat it takes from the fileWhat it does with it
          
  
          The assemblercard name; device.part and family; vendor; device.logic.native_width; synthesis.nowidelut; DSP block count and multiplier list; the board pin tablewrites the Verilog top, the build script and the pin file for that card (the previous page shows its runs; the Assembler page sets out the families and flags)
          
  
          The mirror VMthe card name only, plus a cell count you give itmakes the VM grid the same shape a real build of that many cells would have, so a program that could never be built is refused in the VM too
          
  
          The card-fit check (the compiler and placer pages)whether the chip counts LUT4s or ALMs; the totals; where the DSP and block-memory columns areworks out how many cell positions the card holds and whether a compiled design fits
          

          

          ← The Verilog and the card split, with the assembler's runsThe assembler, which reads the MAN file →The placer, which uses the card-fit check →
          


          The mirror VM, live
          

          This demo uses the Mustang file (the mirror needs only a card name, so either file would give the same grid). The mirror takes the name and a cell count, and lays out the grid the same way the assembler would: near-square, filled row by row. The add program (27 cells, spread over rows 2 to 6 and columns 1 to 14) is then checked against it. Pick a cell count. Dark squares are positions a real build would have; orange squares are the program's cells; a red outline is a program cell sitting where no real cell would exist.
          

          

          

          

          The same check runs when the Workbench's "set target" is used and when the LLVM command-line tool is given --man with --cells. The mirror VM gets its own page later, and that page will link back here.
          

          The mirror checks shape only: does every cell sit on a position a real build of that size would have, and do none share one. It does not check that the chip has room. That second question belongs to the card-fit check and the cost table below.
          


          What a cell costs on this card
          

          The Tang Nano file carries a table of measured costs: each flex-family cell was built at six widths and counted by the open synthesis tool, and a straight line (or a curve for the multiplier) was fitted through the points. Pick a cell and a width. The page reads the table at measured widths and uses the fit between them.
          

          

          

          

          The count above is plain division of the chip's 20,736 LUT4s by the cell's cost. It ignores wiring, the shared connections between cells and the clock, so it is a ceiling for the arithmetic and not a promise that this many will place.
          


          Positions the card holds
          

          The card-fit check costs a design in positions, one per cell instantiated, at a measured cost per position, and keeps a margin (80% of the chip). The costs below were measured on the older cardinal cell shells, not on the flex cells above, so the two tables answer different questions. Notice how few positions even the cheapest shell gets on the Tang Nano against how many there are LUT4s.
          

          


          What the card says it can do
          

          The capabilities block is a list of yes/no facts about the card, each with a second flag for whether this project has actually used it yet.
          

          

          


          How the files are made, and how far to trust them
          

          
  
          Tang Nano 20K: generated
          
  
          Mustang F100: assembled by hand
          

          

          Where the generator can read a fact from a source (the chip database, the synthesis tool's own cell library) it does, and the file records where each fact came from. Where a fact is a decision (the no-wide-LUT default), the file says whose decision and which measurements back it.
          


          Gaps, plainly
          

            
  
          • Nothing reads the capabilities block yet. The README describes it as the way a loader or generator refuses features a card lacks. A search of the Python in nano/ and tools/ finds it written by the two file generators and read by no tool; the real refusals above come from the synthesis and device.dsp fields.
            • 
  
          • Nothing reads the cost table in the file except its own generator and a test. The assembler does not use it to refuse a design that is too big.
            • 
  
          • The Mustang file is thin for the newer routes: no word width, no multiplier list, no cost table.
            • 
  
          • The Tang Nano file was never tested on the board. Its own verification block says the schematic is not checked and no bitstream has been loaded on the board by this project.
            • 
  
          • SHAPE and BITSTREAM, the other two of the four artifacts, were not run for this page.
            • 

          


          Scope. Section sizes, field values, cost tables, fits, budgets and the mirror results are read from the two files and from nano/card_fit_v1.py and nano/vm_mirror_v1.py by docs/teaching/capture_rtl_v1.py. The descriptions of what each section is for are written from the files' own notes and from reading the code that uses them; the "nothing reads it" statements come from a text search and could miss indirect use. No hardware, synthesis or placement was run for this page.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§22 / 28
          The Assembler: Four Cell Families and Its Flags
          The tool that turns a program and a card into hardware files has to choose what kind of cell to build from. The four families (standalone, carrier, sub, flex) side by side, by what each can and cannot do, and the flags that steer the assembler.
          

          



          The assembler is the tool that turns a program and a card into hardware files. Before it can do that it has to choose what kind of cell to build from, and the design has four kinds, grown one from another. They are not four lists of the same cells. Each family makes a different trade, so each can do things the others cannot. This page sets them side by side, then shows the assembler building from each.
          


          The four families
          

          Names run in the order they were made: the standalone cell (v4), the carrier (v4c), the sub or stripped cell (v4s) and the flex cell (v4sa). Pick one to see what it is, which cell kinds it has, what the assembler builds from it, and what it costs.
          

          

          


          What each family can and cannot do
          

          This table is the point of the page. Every yes and no in the first block is read from the adder's Verilog file in each family (its real ports and parameters); the rest come from the file headers and the measured sizes. Shaded cells are where a family differs from the one before it.
          

          

          


          Which cell kinds each family has
          

          

          


          Try it: what do you need?
          

          Tick what you need from the cell. The page keeps the families that can do all of it. When nothing is left, that is the design's trade showing: no family has every ability, because the abilities cost area or fix timing.
          

          

          

          


          How the assembler builds from each
          

          These are four real runs of tools/project_assemble_v1.py. Notice that the family is chosen by flags, and that the routes are not equally capable.

          The assembler's flags
          

          Most programs are run by pressing a button. The assembler is run by a command line, and the flags on that line are how you steer it: which card, which family, which program, how wide, which synthesis options.  of them are listed below, with the text the tool prints for each. Type to filter, or open a group.
          

          

          


          Build a command
          

          Choose a route, a card and some flags. The page writes the command and checks it against the tool's rules. Each complaint below is the tool's own message, captured from a real run of that combination, not written for this page.
          

          
  
          
    
          
    
          
    
          
    
          
      
          
    
          
  
          
  
          
    
          
    
          
  
          

          


          Gaps, plainly
          

            
  
          • Only the sub and flex routes build a program. A program file (--icm) is accepted only with -s sub or -s flex. The standalone and carrier routes write arrays of cells for the Intel Quartus tool; the program is loaded into them afterwards by the host tools, not by the assembler.
            • 
  
          • Sizes are quoted, not measured here. No synthesis tool is installed in this workspace. The numbers come from the project's own tables and ledger.
            • 
  
          • The carrier numbers are the whole carrier, with all fifteen cores present (fourteen at first; the division core took slot 15) and one switched on. The "lean" figures in the standalone table replace the shift chain with empty stubs, so they are lower bounds for a core, not working cells.
            • 
  
          • Some flags are accepted and do nothing. On the program route, --logiclock and -P are not refused the way they are on the chain route, and a real run with --logiclock wrote files identical to the run without it. The tool's own error text says those options belong to the carrier lineage; on the program route nothing says so.
            • 
  
          • Older shells exist. The default route can still array the earlier unicell_super shells (--shell v3, --shell v4); they are older lineage, not a fifth family, and this page does not cover them.
            • 

          

          Scope. Port counts, parameters, yes/no flags, cell-kind lists and the carrier's selectable cores are parsed from the Verilog files by docs/teaching/capture_asm_v1.py; the four routes are real runs of the assembler. The one-line descriptions are written from each family's own file headers and sub/README.md. Sizes are LUT4 counts from synth_gowin read from nano/card_fit_v1.py, the Tang Nano MAN and ledger #898, not re-measured, and counts of how many fit are plain division ignoring wiring. Nothing here was simulated or synthesised.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§23 / 28
          Mixing Families: Sub Blocks, the Bridge and Rings
          Some blocks can be built from the small, fast, fixed-time sub cells while the rest stays flex. Where the two meet the assembler inserts a bridge by itself. What the bridge does, how the Composer and Workbench show it, and how rings are stopped in each family, with numbers measured on the generated hardware.
          

          



          UniCell has more than one kind of cell. Most of this manual uses flex cells, which talk by handshake: "I have a word" / "I took it". The sub cells are stripped down: they take exactly one clock, never say "wait", and cannot queue anything. That makes them small and fast, but a sub block next to a flex block needs a translator. That translator is the bridge, and the assembler puts it in for you.
          


          flex block (handshake)sub block (fixed time, no handshake)bridge (inserted by the assembler)
          

          The Composer and the Workbench colour blocks this way. The VM itself cannot run a fixed-time sub block faithfully, so it runs every cell in its normal mode and the colours only show which family each block is built from; the real difference appears in the generated hardware.
          


          What the bridge does
          

          
  
          flexblock A
          +1000
          
  
          bridge intakes a word only if idle
          
  
          subblock B
          +234
          
  
          bridge outcatches & HOLDS the word
          
  
          flexblock C
          +5
          

          

          A sub block can neither refuse a word nor make one wait. So the bridge lets one word in at a time, catches the result, and holds it until the flex side says "taken". Only then does it let the next word in. The held word is the same thing as the measure point in a ring (below): the place where fast fixed-time maths becomes something a handshake cell can compare, check or store.
          


          Watch real words go through
          

          This is the generated hardware for A → B → C, simulated. Each bar is one word, from the clock the host handed it in to the clock the flex side took the result out (it waits its turn, because only one word is in the sub block at a time). Every result was checked: x + 1000 + 234 + 5.
          

          


          


          What you do, and what the tools do
          

          

          YouThe tools
          

          In the Composer: pick a block, set cell family to sub.The block turns blue; the side panel lists the bridges that will be inserted, and says so plainly if the design cannot be split (for example a sub block with two inputs).
          

          Or write "family": "sub" on a placement in the design file.project_assemble_v1.py --icm FILE notices the tag, builds each region with its own generator, and wires a bridge on every crossing.
          

          Nothing else.The Workbench colours the same blocks; the VM runs them in its normal mode.
          

          

          python3 tools/project_assemble_v1.py -s flex --icm nano/examples/mixed_flex_sub_flex_v1.icm-hier.json --top mix --output out/
# Mixed families: flex0(flex), sub1(sub), flex2(flex)   Bridges inserted: 2
          


          Standard and carrier blocks (ledger #1160, #1162)
          

          A block can also be tagged std (the standard line, built on the standalone cell shells) or carrier (the standard line on the trimmed VIXeN carrier). These cells hand a word over differently: a cell offers a word (a level that stays up), the receiver is told one clock when it arrives, and "taken" is a one-clock event, not a level. The join to a flex block is two small pieces of wiring with no memory of their own: one turns the flex "valid and ack" into the standard "arrived" pulse (only when the standard cell says it is ready), the other turns the standard "offering" into a flex valid and sends back the one-clock "taken" pulse. The assembler puts them in on every crossing, and a standard block next to a carrier block gets one of each in series.
          

          The first test of this found something worth knowing: a standard cell reads "taken" as an event. Wire a flex ack (which is high whenever the flex cell is empty) straight to it and the cell never fires at all. The adapter therefore sends "taken" only in the clock the word actually moves. A test shows the deadlock when it is wired the wrong way.
          

          python3 tools/project_assemble_v1.py -s flex --icm nano/examples/mixed_flex_std_flex_v1.icm-hier.json --top mix --output out/
# Mixed families: flex0(flex), std1(std), flex2(flex)   Bridges inserted: 2
          

          Checked in simulation with real cells, 30 words each, with the output ready all the time and stalling at random, every word equal to x + the sum of the blocks' constants, in order: flex-std-flex, flex-carrier-flex, flex-std-carrier-flex and flex-carrier-std-flex. Refused with a reason: standard or carrier next to a sub block (put a flex block between them), a core the standard line does not have (it has ram, adder, branch and accumulator), a host-named cell inside a standard or carrier block, and more than one carrier block.
          


          Rings in each family
          

          A ring feeds its own result back in, so it needs a way to stop. Both families get one, and both were measured on the same looped CORDIC (the first five results are identical in the two; they match the independent model).
          

          

          Sub ring, in plain words (Alan's design): let the word go all the way round once, halt it at the measure point, check, then refire it. The ring never has to know how long it is, because the word's arrival is the signal. Checking while it is still moving is always at least one clock too late, so the hold is the honest place to check.
          


          Limits to know
          

            

          • One word in flight per sub block. A long sub block therefore runs at one word per (its length + about 3 clocks), not one per clock. A queued bridge could fix that; it is not built.
            • 

          • A sub block must have exactly one entry and one exit crossing, and no host ports of its own. The assembler refuses anything else and says why.
            • 

          • Flex, sub, standard and carrier blocks can be mixed (standard and carrier cannot touch a sub block directly). The nano shell still has no adapter. Standard and carrier blocks only have four cores: ram, adder, branch, accumulator.
            • 

          • Simulated only; not yet run on the board. Clock speed of the mixed design is not measured.
            • 

          

          Where this comes from: ledger #1111 (sub ring), #1112/#1113 (the bridge), #1114 (mixed blocks), #1160/#1162 (standard and carrier blocks). Code: sub/verilog/flex_sub_bridge_v1.v, sub/verilog/flex_std_adapter_v1.v, tools/flexsub_mixed_v2.py. Tests: tests/vm/test_flex_std_adapter_v1.py, test_mixed_std_regions_v1.py, tests/vm/test_flex_sub_bridge_v1.py, test_mixed_blocks_v1.py, test_sub_ring_v1.py.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§24 / 28
          Saving a Running Design and Putting It Back
          A running design keeps words waiting inside its cells. Write them all down at one instant and you can stop, switch off, and later continue exactly where it was, even on a different machine: the real card, the simulator or the VM. What is in the file, why it refuses a wrong design, and the moves that were run.
          

          

          A design that is running holds a little memory in every cell: which words are waiting, and what they are. If you could write all of that down at one instant, you could stop the machine, switch it off, and later put it back exactly as it was. That is a saved state. UniCell can do this on the real card, in the simulator and in the VM, and move a state between them.
          


          What is saved, and what is not
          

          The wiring of the design lives in the bitstream, and the cell settings arrive from a configuration pulse, so neither is saved. Only the dynamic registers are: each cell's "I am holding a word" flags and the words themselves. For the LaTeX example y = (z² + 12345) mod 65521 that is 15 cells and 678 bits.
          


          One file, that says what it is
          

          The raw image from the card is just 256 bytes of bits; what each bit means lives in a second file (the scan map), and losing it would make the image useless. So the tool tools/scan_image_v1.py writes one JSON file (format unicell-state-v1) holding the design name, the formula, a fingerprint of the register layout, the point where the run was cut, the closing register, and for every cell and register its name, width and value. A plain-words flag live says which values matter (a data register counts as live when its own pending flag is set). The flag is advisory; the bits are exact.
          

          Loading rebuilds the bits by name against the target design, and refuses, saying what differs, if a cell, register, width or the layout fingerprint does not match. A state for the wrong design can not be pushed in by mistake.
          


          The moves that were run
          

          

          FromToResult
          

          real cardsimulatorcontinues to the model's answer
          

          simulatorreal cardPASS (after power off and a fresh bitstream load)
          

          real cardVMcontinues to the model's answer
          

          VMreal cardPASS, word 25408 = model 25408, 0 retries (ledger #1161)
          

          

          One design, one cut for the VM leg, one card. The state file, not the machine, is what carries the work.
          


          Why the VM needs a translator
          

          The VM is not a copy of the card, clock by clock, so tools/vm_state_bridge_v1.py bridges four differences. The VM divider works out its answer up front and counts down; the card's divider is stepped, so a half-finished card division is finished with the divider's own rule. A join fires on the card when both inputs wait, but the VM takes them one at a time. The assembler removes the priority cells that the VM keeps. And the card's constants are rams that offer their value forever, while the VM's are loaded once and ran dry in round 4 until they were marked as fixed. The bridge refuses VM states the card cannot hold, such as an operand that has only half arrived.
          


          A lesson in it
          

          Every "obvious" step here failed once before it worked: a constant served twice, a wrong answer above 32 bits (the hardware wraps before the remainder), a handshake that needs a one-clock pulse and not a level. The checks that caught them were all the same: run it, and compare with a plain model.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§25 / 28
          UniCell Bench: Building and Running on a Card From One Page
          One local page that holds the picker, the two shells, the build and card buttons, the results and an ICM panel that makes a new build folder for a chosen card. What each part does, how the MAN file chooses the flow, and what has and has not been measured.
          

          

          Building for a real card used to mean typing the same cd, make and OpenOCD lines again and again. UniCell Bench puts them on one page, and the same page can start from an ICM file.
          


          The whole pipeline
          

          Drawing (composer), LaTeX, DSL or LLVM IR → ICM file → either the VM, or the assembler → a build folder → the card. The Bench is the last two steps in one window.
          


          What is on the page
          

          

          PartWhat it does
          

          DesignsEvery build folder in your demo folder. Click one and both shells cd into it.
          

          Build shellEnter the openXC7 environment, check it, make, and load into the card's SRAM (it asks first; it never writes flash).
          

          Card shellButtons for the kit's OpenOCD scripts: read, freeze at a clock, release, save, load, round trip, sweep. Only scripts the folder really has are shown.
          

          ResultsThe build verdict (timing passed or failed) and the files the scripts wrote, decoded: a card read, PASS/FAIL for a round trip.
          

          ICM panelPick an ICM file and a card; it makes a new build folder inside the demo folder, and the Designs list picks it up.
          

          


          The card decides how it is built
          

          Each card's MAN file has a flow: openxc7 (Kintex, open tools), gowin-apicula (Tang Nano) or export-only (closed tools such as Arria 10: you get a plain Verilog folder and a README, and synthesise it yourself). A new open-source card is a new MAN file. The MAN file can also hold a startup command that the page asks you for once and keeps only on your PC.
          


          What an ICM run on the Kintex card is
          

          The generated project wraps the design in a small runner: it feeds test words into the entries, counts what comes out of each exit, and keeps a signature and the clock of the last word. A script reads that over JTAG and checks each exit against what the VM says it should be.
          


          One rule for a constant, and which VM checks the card
          

          A ram cell that has a preloaded value, is not marked fixed and has nothing feeding it gives its value once and is then empty. That is the original (standard) reading, and every family now follows it. If you want a value that is always there, such as a CORDIC angle constant, mark the cell fixed (fixed_mode 1). The CORDIC example cordic_z_convergence_v2 does exactly that for its eight angle constants; the four zero references stay one-shot because the branch cell keeps the first value it sees as its reference.
          

          The VM that the card is compared with is the original grid (FlexGrid v1). A second grid, FlexGrid v2, exists only to reproduce older results that relied on the old flex behaviour; new work does not use it. When the hardware counts two equal words in a row as two words and the VM's list merged them, the hardware's count is taken, because the VM is corrected to the hardware, not the other way round. Any other difference is still reported as a disagreement.
          


          What has and has not been shown
          

          

          ShownNot yet
          

          Freeze, read, save and load on the Kintex card (several clocks, PASS). A whole ICM path: ICM file → panel → build → load → fed over JTAG → answers equal the VM, for the small relay chain, the 4-input reduction tree and the 4-stage CORDIC with fixed constants (two input sets each; CORDIC 10 1 2 → 2736 2727 2728 and 14 100 3 → 2740 2826 2729).Save and load inside the runner; the sub, standard and mixed families on Xilinx.
          

          In simulation the generated hardware agrees with the VM for 17 of the 26 example designs (the rest are refused with a reason, cannot be compared, or were explained).CORDIC with an input of 0 or with negative inputs on the card; a held constant feeding a multiplier.
          

          The page works in a headless browser test and on the author's PC for picking, shells, environment check, build verdicts and the ICM panel.Any design beyond the examples; widths other than 32.

          Imago UniCell · Teaching Manual§26 / 28
          The Cells, One Page Each
          19 kinds of cell, each with a page: capability, a diagram of what is inside, the Verilog, and which families have it.
          

          Each cell kind has a page of its own: what it can do, how data moves through it, a diagram drawn from the real Verilog, the parts it is made of, the size, and the full source, for each family that has it. The family tags show where it exists: v4 standalone, v4c carrier, v4s sub, v4sa flex. The Assembler page compares the families themselves.
          

          Remembering
          
ramHolds one word.v4v4cv4sv4sa
latchHolds one bit.v4v4cv4sv4sa
sequencerSteps through four stored values.v4v4cv4sv4sa

          

          Arithmetic
          
adderA plus B, or A minus B.v4v4cv4sv4sa
accumulatorA running total with up and down pulses.v4v4cv4sv4sa
mulA times B.v4v4cv4sv4sa
divDivides one word by another.v4v4cv4sv4sa

          

          Deciding
          
compareIs the input at least the threshold?v4v4cv4sv4sa
branchCompares, then chooses where to send.v4v4cv4sv4sa

          

          Joining and splitting
          
mergeJoins two paths into one.v4v4cv4sa
priorityChooses between four inputs by a rule.v4v4cv4sa
routerSends one value to both outputs.v4sv4sa

          

          Wiring
          
cornerTurns a lane.v4v4cv4sv4sa
crossLets two lanes cross.v4v4cv4sv4sa

          

          Reshaping words
          
shiftShifts a word left or right.v4v4cv4s
shift_stageA shift fixed when the cell is built.v4sv4sa
maskZeroes chosen nibbles.v4v4cv4sv4sa

          

          The gate, and control
          
nanoThe universal two-input gate.v4v4cv4sv4sa
commandTriggers and programs other cells.v4v4c

          

          Scope. 19 kinds across four families, 74 Verilog file entries embedded in full (the corner and cross tiles in the sub and flex families show the ram cell the generator builds them from). The kinds are counted from file names: shift and mask exist in the older families as add-on blocks inside every cell rather than as cells, and the page for each says so.
